preface: # Reality
Where real macOS differed from what Arbor's stand-ins, tests or authors expected: every known case, what was expected, what happened, how it
was found, whether the stand-ins can do the same by now, and what would go red if Arbor forgot it again.
**Why there is such a list.** Arbor's logic talks to macOS only through a few protocols (`Sources/ArborKit/Platform`), and thousands of tests run the real
controller against stand-ins for them (`Sources/ArborTesting`; `Sources/arbor-fakemac` plays whole Mac shell scripts on Linux). They all pass. The
serious faults were found on real Macs all the same, because the stand-ins are politer than macOS: they report everything, once, in one order,
at once, and nobody else moves a window. A test against a stand-in proves that Arbor does the right thing in the world the stand-in makes up. This
list is how far that world is from the real one.
a person, apps, macOS itself
──────────────────────────────  real behaviour: order, silence, delay, other actors
AX · Input · UI · App            macOS-only code. No headless test runs it: "below the seam"
══════════════════════════════  THE SEAM: WindowSystem, OverlayPresenter, Scheduler, StateStore …
Controller · ArborCore           what the tests run, on stand-ins: FakeWindowSystem, FakeOverlays, ManualScheduler
**How to read an entry.** *Where* says in which storey the difference bit. "At the seam" means that it shows in what crosses the protocols, so a stand-in can play it
to the controller, and if it does not yet, that is work to do. "Below the seam" means that the macOS-only code met it: no stand-in can play it, and only
a check on real windows guards it. *Stand-ins play it* names the switch or helper. *Guard* names what goes red: a test, a scenario, a recorded trace
that is replayed on every platform, or a step on real windows (`e2e:`). CI runs `arbor-e2e` and `e2e-drag.sh` by itself; a step of any other script is marked
"by hand": it guards only when somebody starts the script, and some of those scripts have never run on a Mac (see the end of this page).
*Touches*, in the line under the heading, names the detectors of the viable gate (`docs/VIABLE.md`, section 5) that a person's trouble would set off: what they would see, not
where the fault lies. A case that touches none is no less true; the gate has no eye for it.

**One kind is not like the others.** Under [never-exercised](#never-exercised) nothing differed, because nothing, or not enough, was tried: each case is a feature that ships switched on, or within reach of a key or the

menu, whose macOS half has never had a key pressed or a hand laid on it on a real Mac, or only in passing: by something other than its own check, or by its own check once, with posted events, started by hand. Each says

exactly what has run, and says "by the spec's own words" where that is the source. It is here because it is the same debt: what is known about it is known from the stand-ins. Such a case shrinks as its check runs: what
differed becomes cases of the other kinds, what held is said, and the entry goes when nothing is left that nobody knows.

**What this list cannot see.** It counts where a Mac differed from the stand-ins. The first person who worked with Arbor quit it and went back to macOS's own tiling, and in nine of the ten complaints that were written down the stand-ins
and the Mac agree: Arbor did what the specs said, or what had been overruled and was not yet built. They have a table of their own, with what held Arbor to each:
[What the first person at a desk met](#what-the-first-person-at-a-desk-met).
**How to keep it.**
1. A real Mac surprised you: add an entry to `collab/reality.json` in the pull request that cures it, or at once with `"copes": "open"` if there is no cure yet.
Say what was expected and by whom (a test, the fake, a comment), what happened, with numbers, how it was seen, and in `"touches"` which detectors it would set off.
2. A cure is finished when the next person cannot undo it unnoticed. At the seam: teach the stand-in the bad manner, write the test that fails without the
cure, name both. Below the seam: name the step on real windows that CI runs, and say `"modelled": "cannot"`.
3. Run `scripts/reality-ledger.py`: it looks every name up (a switch that was renamed, a test that was deleted, a step nobody runs any more), counts, and writes this
file. `make lint` fails when a name is gone or this file is stale.
4. **Your lint fails here and you never touched the ledger?** You reworded a step, or renamed a test, a stand-in's switch or a file, that a case names as its guard, its knob or its
source. Under each ✘ a line that begins with → says which field of which case in `collab/reality.json` to change, and to what. Then run the script and commit both files.
5. Nothing from a person's Mac goes in here beyond the fact itself: no names, no paths, no apps somebody runs, no logs.

entries.expected: What a process pressed is let go of when the process ends.
entries.happened: Nobody else lets go of it: the window server goes on believing that it is down until a person presses that very button or key. A ⌘ that stays down turns the next Q into ⌘Q.
entries.found: Writing the pointer tool and the harness that cleans up after a script that died.
guards: e2e: calm finds both keys down and lets go of them
e2e: Arbor is killed in the middle of a ⌃⌥-drag
e2e: the killed process leaves no tap behind
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/lib.sh ends every run, killed or not, with `pointer calm`, which lets go of whatever macOS says is down; a killed Arbor's taps go with its process.

entries.expected: A helper tool that passes the type-check against the stand-ins for Apple's frameworks compiles on a Mac.
entries.happened: In a program of one file, what a `guard let` binds at the top level is a local variable. A function that reads one captures it and cannot be handed to C as a callback (`AXObserverCreate`). The compiler says so only when it generates code, which the type-check never does, and the stand-in's callback is an ordinary closure. The run on the Mac ended at the first compile.
entries.found: A probe's first run on a hosted Mac; the same error from two small files on Linux with `-emit-sil`.
entries.copes: open

entries.expected: A key that is held sends presses again and again, so a view would run on.
entries.happened: Carbon sends one press however long the key is down. One note says this was checked on a Mac, a later one that it has not been seen and is only believed: they disagree about the evidence, not about the belief.
entries.found: "Checked on a Mac", says the review of the input code, without naming a script. scripts/mac-shell/input-taps.sh posts ten auto-repeats and counts the commands.
guards: e2e: the command ran once: shortcuts do not repeat
entries.copes: Controller.shortcut gets a press and a release and does nothing more while the key stays down.

entries.expected: Arbor either has Accessibility or has not, and an Arbor started again by its watchdog has what it had.
entries.happened: Started as a child process Arbor answers with the permission of the terminal, or of the hosted Mac's agent. The same binary in a bundle opened through Launch Services answers for itself: it has none, as on a newcomer's Mac. A bundled Arbor started again as a child would be the child of a process that no longer exists; and `open` hands on only the environment variables it is told to.
entries.found: Mac shell scripts on a hosted Mac: the first launch in pictures and the bundled watchdog.
guards: e2e: another Arbor took over, with the same home folder and socket
e2e: the watchdog starts Arbor again
entries.copes: Watchdog.run starts a bundled Arbor again through `open -n --env`, so that macOS sees the app itself asking.

entries.expected: A click in the middle of Arbor's menu bar item opens its menu, as the scripts' helper and the fake Mac of the time agreed.
entries.happened: With something docked the item is a row of buttons, and a plain click in its middle presses one of them. The helper had been wrong for real Macs since those buttons shipped; it showed, as 82 red checks, only when the fake Mac learnt the buttons. A green rehearsal agrees with the fake of that hour. On 2026-10-15 hosted Macs showed how far it went: twelve scripts clicked the middle of the item to "open the menu", and the middle is Show the Desktop. None of their pictures showed a menu, and the view changed under the steps that followed. A right click opens the menu wherever it lands: seen in four pictures since. All twelve are mended; `input-taps.sh` and `check-desktop.sh` have not run again.
entries.found: Rehearsing the Mac shell scripts against the fake Mac at two display sizes. Then a sweep, on hosted Macs, of the checks that had never run.
entries.copes: Sources/arbor-fakemac/World+Menu.swift lays the row of buttons out as the app does, so a rehearsal shows the slip; the last button and a right click open the menu.

entries.expected: Whatever brings a window to the front is followed by a focus report, so pinned and summoned windows need looking at only then.
entries.happened: A click in the window that already has the keyboard brings it to the front and reports no change of focus. Every click in the editor one is working in buried the pinned call until the next layout. Whether a real click brings the window in front of another app's raised window is still open.
entries.found: Rehearsing a real-window script on the fake Mac found the fault in Arbor. The two scripts that would show it on real windows ran on hosted Macs on 2026-10-15 and could show nothing of it: the raise did not reach the front there (raise-does-not-lift-a-window-over-the-active-apps-key-window).
guards: e2e: after clicking the browser again
e2e: after a second click on the editor nothing covers it either
entries.copes: Controller.lookAfterPinnedWindowsAfterAPress looks at every press (`pointerPressed`), every 0.2 s while the button is down and three more times after.

entries.expected: A press on a window tells Arbor something about that window.
entries.happened: After a press and a release on a title bar no event about any window reaches Arbor.
entries.found: A trace of a real click on a test window on a hosted Mac.
entries.copes: WindowGrab.classify decides nothing while the window stands still.

entries.expected: A plain click on the bare Desktop is waited for by nobody but Finder, so asking what is under the pointer is enough to keep it from macOS.
entries.happened: People click the wallpaper to be rid of an open menu, Spotlight, Control Centre, a Dock stack, a popover or a list of completions. With the guard on, that click would reach nobody and the thing would stay open; an item of Arbor's own menu hanging over the Desktop could not be clicked, Finder would not become active or clear its selection, and an icon would light up when the button comes up, not when it goes down.
entries.found: A second reader of the macOS-only code, after the guard had been merged switched on. Nobody has seen the guard at work on a Mac, and the levels of menus, Spotlight and Mission Control have not been measured.
guards: e2e: session 3: a click on the Desktop does not sweep the windows away
entries.copes: Settings.guardDesktopClicks ships false until the guard has been seen on a Mac; PointerSurface.whatMayBeWaiting gives the click back unless everything above the palettes is what a Mac at rest has there.

entries.expected: Nothing but Arbor, the apps and the person moves a window, and whoever moves one is reported. The Desktop and the gaps between docked windows are safe to click.
entries.happened: "Click wallpaper to reveal desktop" (macOS 14 and later; an absent key means on) sweeps every window to the sides of the screen at one click on the wallpaper or in a gap, and the next click only brings them back. Measured on macOS 26.6: frames at 12,43 and 518,176 went to -482,-17 and 1012,82, with 2 to 4% of each window left in view. It is a picture: the window server lists them there, and goes on listing them with the sizes they had, whatever becomes of them; Accessibility has every window where it is and reports no move. A frame set meanwhile is taken, shows nowhere, does not end the sweep, and is where the window comes back to. They go left, right, up or down, until 12 points show. What brings them back: a click on the wallpaper, a press on a strip, ⌘Tab, an app that comes forward. What does not: a raise, minimizing and restoring, a window that opens (in view), waiting. F11 is the same thing. The Dock announces both ends (AXExposeShowDesktop, AXExposeExit) 0.2 s late. With the mouse-down, the mouse-up or both swallowed in a session event tap nothing moves; a click with ⇧ sweeps nothing.
entries.found: Mac shell runs with real clicks on a hosted Mac, and a later experiment with its control. A real-window script that clicked the wallpaper swept every window on the Mac aside and failed two checks. A probe that wrote down both views of every window sixty times a second through 22 sweeps.
guards: e2e: session 3: a click on the Desktop does not sweep the windows away
e2e: every window is in view after the second click
e2e: every window is where it was, by the window server
e2e: no stage went up over the bare desktop
entries.copes: SweptAside.isSwept tells a sweep by the two views disagreeing. Arbor goes by Accessibility and lays out as ever, unseen, without a stage over the bare desktop (`Controller.stageTransition`). Settings.guardDesktopClicks keeps the click from macOS, but ships off until it has been seen at work on a Mac. As Arbor comes, `doctor` and the welcome window only name the macOS switch (`MacSwitch.clickWallpaper`).

entries.expected: A click count of 2 on a mouse-down means a double-click.
entries.happened: A click on a title bar followed at once by a drag, and a drag with a double tap, arrive with a click count of 2 as well: the window would be framed at the second mouse-down and the drag reach nobody. macOS counts on, 1, 2, 3, 4, so every even count is a double-click.
entries.found: A review of the double-click feature, by reading. The feature is not in the tree.
entries.copes: open

entries.expected: A click during a peek, with ⌃⌥ held, reaches the window under it as a click.
entries.happened: The app underneath would open a contextual menu (⌃-click), macOS would hide the app that had the keyboard (⌥-click on another app's window), and a ⌃-click may arrive as the other button's.
entries.found: Read in comments in the source and in the harness; the run that showed it is not named.
entries.copes: PeekOutlinePanel takes the click meant for what it outlines, from either button, and only reports it (`peekOutlineClicked`).

entries.expected: The window that gets the keyboard is in front by then. One look at the stacking after a focus report (`windowFocused`) is enough, and a panel ordered directly above the focused window stays there. The stand-in brings a window to the front before it reports the focus.
entries.happened: On macOS 26 a clicked window takes the keyboard first and comes to the front afterwards. The focus line, ordered above its window at the focus report, ended up behind it, under other windows' shadows. A pinned window raised at the report was covered again a moment later.
entries.found: Screenshots and checks of the window server's stack from a Mac shell script that drove the focus line on test windows on a hosted Mac, macOS 26.
guards: e2e: the ring is still directly above its window after a click into it
entries.copes: Controller.keepPinsInFront looks when the event is over and twice more, 0.2 s apart, not counting looks with the button down. The focus line is put above its window again at every mouse-up, 0.15 s later and after every update (Sources/ArborKit/UI/FocusRingPanel.swift).

entries.expected: Writing a reply to a socket whose reader has gone fails with an error.
entries.happened: It raises SIGPIPE, and the default is to die on the spot. ⌃C on `arborctl state`, or any client that hung up early, killed Arbor with windows out of view.
entries.found: A review of the app shell, then the real-window runner, which hangs up twenty times.
guards: e2e: clients that hang up without reading the reply
entries.copes: ProcessGuards.prepareProcess ignores SIGPIPE first thing in the process, so the write fails with an error.

entries.expected: Time only goes forward, so the time of day will do for "how long ago".
entries.happened: With the clock set back an hour, every move the person made of a window would count as Arbor's own echo for an hour. In the same way the keyboard leads every shortcut until the next focus change, because how long the focus has rested is still reckoned by the time of day.
entries.found: Reviews of the Accessibility layer and the app shell, by reading. Nobody has set a clock back.
entries.copes: EchoFilter.judge is fed the system's uptime, which never goes backwards, and drops an expectation from the future. How long the focus has rested is still reckoned by the time of day.

entries.expected: A window that has closed is gone from the window server's list. The fake Mac forgets it.
entries.happened: A test window that closes stays in the list, off screen, because it is not released when closed.
entries.found: The first comparison, line by line, of one script played on a hosted Mac (six runs, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768) and in a rehearsal on Linux. The difference was seen; its cause is a reading.
entries.copes: Sources/arbor-fakemac/World+TestApps.swift is what would have to change; there is nothing to mend in Arbor. What real apps with one window make of it: one-window-apps-show-the-same-number-again.

entries.expected: A window that is closed leaves the window server's list with the frame it had.
entries.happened: macOS lets it shrink as it goes: 520×300 became 512×296 and 510×294 in the 200 ms before it left. Read as moves, that is a window somebody moved and then closed.
entries.found: The sabotage run on a hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2, on 2026-10-15, where a window closed on purpose was reported by two detectors.
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/jolts.py leaves out what a window does in its last 600 ms within 24 points of where it was, as it does for a window that opens.

entries.expected: Any press on a window brings it forward and gives it the keyboard.
entries.happened: macOS does not bring a window forward for a ⌘-click. A window of an app in the background can be moved by ⌘-dragging its title bar without coming forward, and the close, minimize and zoom buttons work without bringing their window forward.
entries.found: Notes in scripts/mac-shell/input-taps.sh and compat-extras.sh, which try it on real apps.
entries.copes: AXWindowSystem goes by reports, not by presses: a window that moves is followed whoever has the keyboard.

entries.expected: A control's Accessibility frame lies inside its window, at a place a script can know.
entries.happened: In a form laid out by SwiftUI what is scrolled out of view still has a place, which may lie outside the window, over something else. A switch's element may be the switch alone or its whole line with the label. Places move with the version of macOS, the font and the text.
entries.found: Writing the real-window script for the settings window and its tool.
guards: e2e: outside the window: not pressed
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/shots-F12.sh declines to press a point outside the window; nothing for Arbor to do.

entries.expected: The "destroyed" notification names the window that went.
entries.happened: A destroyed Accessibility element answers nothing any more, its window number included. The number has to travel with the subscription.
entries.found: Writing the tools that watch real windows' notifications.
entries.copes: AXWindowSystem.makeRecord registers each window's notifications with the window number as their reference value, which is what `windowDestroyed` carries.

entries.expected: Windows Arbor does not arrange are no concern of Arbor's, and an app's alert opens where it can be seen.
entries.happened: Apps place alerts and panels relative to their main window. If Arbor keeps that window just past a corner of the display, "Save changes?" may open out there too: the Dock icon bounces, the app ignores clicks, quitting stalls, and the app looks hung. Whether AppKit pulls such windows into view first is not known for real apps, and nobody has seen yet whether a plain panel calls itself a dialog.
entries.found: A review of the Accessibility layer, reasoned from how AppKit centres alerts. Built and unit-tested, not yet seen on a Mac: the real-window runner's step with a dialog only says what happened and cannot fail the run.
entries.copes: AXWindowSystem.bringIntoViewIfDialog moves such a dialog to the middle of the display, once (`StrayDialog` decides), or lets it wait while a view is held, until `bringInStrayDialogs(ofApp:)`. The fake only counts dialogs that wait: they have no frame and no window.

entries.expected: A display that is plugged in again might be a new display to macOS. Or the other way round: the same vendor, product and serial number are the same display everywhere.
entries.happened: The same vendor, product and serial number give the same UUID when the display is unplugged and plugged in again, and another serial number is another display. That holds within one run only: another Mac gives the same virtual display another UUID.
entries.found: The displays script with a virtual display on a hosted Mac.
guards: e2e: replugged: the arrangement is the one that went away
e2e: another serial number is another display
entries.copes: Controller.restoreDormantWorkspace gives a display that returns its arrangement back, by its identifier, which is the UUID.

entries.expected: A tool sets the display's mode and the mode stays.
entries.happened: A mode set outside a permanent configuration is undone when the process that set it exits.
entries.found: A comment in the Mac shell harness's app tool.
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/apptool.swift sets the mode through a configuration that is completed for good.

entries.expected: A docked window let go in the band that Arbor leaves to macOS belongs to whoever takes it: if macOS does not take it, it goes home to its slot, in one move, its neighbours untouched, at all three edges. The product owner's answer (board 1.56). **Turned round within the night** (Q29, board 0.4): a plain drag means out, wherever it ends: macOS takes the window, or it floats at its own size where it lies; home is for a ⌘-drag that found no target, and for a slip of under 24 points. By that the top does what is wanted and the sides do not.
entries.happened: On the trunk it differs by edge. Left and right: back to its slot. At the top it is undocked and floats, and its neighbour takes the room.
entries.found: The stories about the standing aside on a model of a Mac under the real Accessibility layer, then played by the product owner in arbor-sim. Not tried on a Mac.
entries.copes: open

entries.expected: Only drags and edge drags change a docked window by hand, so a change of size (`windowChanged`) after a press is an edge resize. macOS's zoom was expected to arrive while the button is down and to move gaps nobody touched, so a rule was written against that. A script's double-click on a title bar is only Arbor's business.
entries.happened: macOS zooms a window whose title bar is double-clicked (or whose green button is ⌥-clicked) to the whole visible frame. A docked one flashed: Arbor put it back 0.26 s later. A floating one covers the docked windows, in one step ((527,472 326×651) to (0,31 1024×674)), which would have hidden every later step of a script. On macOS 26 the resize arrives with the button already up, so it never was taken for an edge drag there. Measured there with real double-clicks at every setting: not set, and set to zoom, the window jumps in one step and a second double-click returns it to the very frame it had; set to fill, it travels in about eight stages over a third of a second, and a second double-click does nothing: fill is no toggle. The press with its count of two reaches whoever listens before the first new frame is reported.
entries.found: A review of the Accessibility layer, the suite of real apps and the drag script with real clicks on a hosted Mac. The trap for scripts came to light in a rehearsal on the fake Mac. Met since by a person at a desk: the maintainer, in a working session with the first build, after Arrange Windows: the window filled the screen for a moment and was put back. It had been ruled a fault the day before (Q22) and was not built.
guards: e2e: double-click the title bar of a docked window
e2e: the window went one way, and did not turn round
entries.copes: WindowGrab.classify: only a press within 10 points of the border begins an edge resize. Controller.standsAsideAfterADoubleClick: what macOS makes of a docked window after a double-click stays, until it is back in its slot or the layout changes. ⌥-click on the green button has a case of its own (macos-moves-a-window-at-its-menu-its-keys-and-the-green-button), and floating windows keep macOS's behaviour by decision.

entries.expected: The end of a drag is one report. `FakeWindowSystem.endDrag`, `loseTheReleaseOfTheDrag` and `dragAndLoseTheRelease` said that the drag had ended or was lost, and nothing before it.
entries.happened: The Accessibility layer reads where the window server has the window, since its app may not have heard yet, and reports that as the person's doing straight before it says that the drag is over (`endGrab`, `releaseWasLost`). In 279 stories played to the real layer on Linux, every end of a drag, every lost one and every end of a resize came straight after such a report. The fake did so for a resize and not for a drag, and the fake Mac only for a drag off a strip.
entries.found: By holding what the fake sends across the seam against what the real layer sends.
entries.copes: Controller.dragEnded goes by the frame it was told last, which with this report is the true one.

entries.expected: The start of a drag (`dragBegan`) is reported before the window moves, then changes and moves of the drag in pairs. The fake's `drag` rests 0.3 s at each point, long enough for a drop target to take.
entries.happened: Arbor learnt of a drag from an Accessibility notice: 0.28 to 0.34 s after the press, after two or three mouse events, with the pointer 40 to 70 points away and the window already moved. It can come after the pointer has stopped, and then only one more mouse event says where the pointer is: a scripted drag without one showed no preview. With a hold of 0.15 s before a target takes, any drag under about 0.45 s was over too soon, and a docked window was undocked and left floating over the others. Whether the figures still hold now that the window server is asked from the press on is said nowhere. **A change by the person before the drag is announced has been recorded:** `changed`, user, between the press and `dragBegan` for the same window in 2 of 58 begun drags in 104 trace files: drag-to-the-second-display (pressed 0.5095, changed 0.8399, begun 0.9186) and drag-to-the-far-edge (0.5608, 0.8204, 0.8990). Both with coarse synthetic steps (45 and 66 points), a virtual second display and the layer of 2026-10-14. A note to a model of a Mac had it that no real layer can say that; it is taken back. Before a resize is announced it has not been seen on a Mac.
entries.found: The traces drag-to-edge and flick-to-edge and scripted drags on a hosted Mac, and a reviewer playing the feature headless. The pointer tool ends every drag with a rest of 0.15 s and one point aside and back for it. The count of 2 in 58: the ledger's keeper's, over the traces in the tree and on the runs' output branches; the two traces are in the tree and were read for this page.
guards: e2e: a drop preview shows while the button is held
entries.copes: WindowGrab.classify decides from the frame at the press, the frame now and the pointer, and the window server is asked at every movement from the press on. A docked window let go before the hold is over goes back to its slot.

entries.expected: "A window follows a drag from the first few points": so a pointer that has gone 24 points with the window standing still is busy with the window's content, and Arbor stops looking (`WindowGrab.patience`). In the stand-ins a window is under the pointer from the first move.
entries.happened: A window may not have moved at the first drag event, and the pointer can be 24 points away before the window server starts to move it. The press is settled as not about the window, both signs of a drag are ignored until the button comes up, and Arbor misses the whole drag: no `dragBegan`, no preview, nothing docks. Seen plainly for the first time in the first run of `check-displays.sh` on a hosted Mac: of four drags of 1,244 to 1,991 points across two displays, in 30 steps each, three were never taken for drags. The windows moved, and nothing was logged, at any level. In the model it is the distance at the first look that finds the window unmoved that counts, not the time: with the window server 100 ms late a pointer 10 or 24 points away is still followed, one 40 points away is lost, for the whole of the drag. What a person would see there: a floating window let go at the edge is not docked, and a docked one dragged out is put back into its slot a quarter of a second after the release. **The cause proven on a hosted Mac, with a control**, on the code before the cure: a floating window dragged 500 points to and fro, a step every 20 ms, six drags of each; the window went along in all 36. In steps of 71 points the drag was seen 1 time of 6, of 45 points 0 of 6, of 29 points 1 of 6; of 22, 14 and 7 points 6 of 6 each. Across two displays, `check-displays.sh`'s own drag in 30 steps (45 to 60 points) 1 of 8, in steps under 20 points 8 of 8. So 26 of 26 at or under the 24 points, 3 of 26 above. The trace has the first look: the press at 0.566 s, the first drag event at 0.737 s and 45.5 points away with the window still in its place, the window's own first change 108 ms after that look, and no drag begun in the whole trace. A test window on a hosted Mac starts to move about 0.25 s after the press and 0.1 s after the first drag event: what the model had guessed, that a window server starts late, is borne out. **The cure proven**: the same probe on the trunk with it, 6 of 6 at all six step sizes and 8 of 8 both ways across two displays, 52 of 52 where it had been 29 of 52; `check-displays.sh` 136 passed and 1 failed where its first run had 110 and 19, and the one is a stale expectation of the script's. The board had it as 1.33.
entries.found: A suite of real-window checks that is not on the trunk yet, in its first run on hosted Macs, beside its rehearsal on Linux, where this was green; the real Accessibility layer run on Linux against a model of a loaded Mac, which lost such drags and showed how; and `check-displays.sh` in its first run on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15. entries.expected: A call to another app returns promptly. In the stand-ins a hung app's `setFrame` returns nil at once, so a hang costs no time.
entries.happened: Accessibility calls are synchronous on the main thread and wait for the app, up to the timeout of 1 s. Moving one window takes four to six calls. A hung app with three docked windows stopped Arbor for 19.5 s at every layout, and 8.8 s were measured for one window. Shortcuts, the menu and the socket were dead meanwhile, and events that were stuck arrived twenty seconds old, after later clicks. Today the first call to an app that has just hung still costs about a second (1.1 s on stopped test windows; 1.06 s, on the main thread, in a later script on a hosted Mac, where the stand-in's hung app answers nil at once). An app that is only busy costs otherwise. On a hosted Mac (macOS 26.6.2), on a build that gives each app a lane of its own and is not on the trunk yet, a test app that works 700 ms and attends 30 ms made no lane late: Arbor's main thread blocks on a read to it, returns the moment the app attends, and the moves that follow are all served within those 30 ms (38 calls, 28 ms). Blocking brings the two into step. What costs is the main thread's reads at notifications: `AXFullScreen` 1,004 ms at worst, `AXFocusedWindow` 660 ms.

entries.expected: A shortcut that the menu, the guide and the panel of shortcuts show as Arbor's is Arbor's for as long as Arbor's item is in the menu bar. A key that Arbor does not hold at the moment does nothing: the guide's table of troubles has the state under "The shortcuts do nothing".
entries.happened: It does whatever the app in front makes of it. On a tester's Mac ⌃⌥A (`arrange`) with a widely used desktop chat app in front archived the open conversation in that app, twice in a row. **Seen since on hosted Macs, by two probes**, Arbor alive and its item in the menu bar in every state. *Another ad-hoc build put over a grant made for the old one, the row in the database still saying "allowed":* on the trunk's Arbor ⌃⌥A reached the app in front, one key down and one up; on the first build's own binary 52 of 52 keys did. *Never granted, waiting at a first launch:* ⌃⌥A twice in a row; 52 of 52. *The permission taken away while it ran, nothing out of view:* ⌃⌥A. And in the states a person asks for: paused, and with shortcuts off for the app in front, 51 of 51 each; with `hotkeysEnabled` false. No such press left a line in Arbor's log, since Arbor does not see the key. It knows the state and says so to whoever asks: without the permission `status` says "waiting for Accessibility permission" and `bindings` "all off without Accessibility permission". **Running, it did not**: 0 of 51 keys reached an app, in each probe, with no event tap installed, as Arbor ships; the key held through 12 repeats and let go: nothing; with a view held and holding still: taken; with secure input on: 0 of 51, though every tap and monitor is deaf then; after the display had slept and woken: 0 of 9. **The holes.** At launch 0.38 s passed between the start and "registered 52 shortcuts"; one ⌃⌥A fell into them and reached the app. Through 21 acts that might register the shortcuts anew Arbor did so twice, at a pause and at the resume, and the only presses an app was given were two during that pause. But that presser made about two presses a second, so a hole under half a second would mostly be missed; and of the first probe's 60 presses only 8 registrations of 1.2 to 1.5 ms fell among them, which is weak. Whether a peek's temporary shortcuts open a hole was not tried. **Which state the person was in is not known**, and nobody has read their log: a new local build over an old grant is the likelier of two candidates, not proven for that session. **The chain that may lie behind that state**, five links, each with its mark. *One, proven* (probes and a check on hosted Macs; macOS 15.7.9 and 26.6.2 do it, 14.8.9 does not): `security import` calls every key it imports "Imported Private Key". `scripts/make-signing-identity.sh` gives codesign leave to use its key by `set-key-partition-list -l "Arbor Local Signing"`, which found none ("The specified item could not be found in the keychain"), and the script called every failure a wrong password: whoever typed the right one read "That is not the keychain's password." three times. *Two, follows for whoever is then without the identity*: `scripts/sign.sh` signs ad hoc when no keychain has the identity, its third choice, and says so in the middle of a build log. By reading, it does not follow from the first link alone: the script imports the identity before it asks, takes nothing out when it fails, and after the third refusal goes on to try a signature, which hosted Macs made without a dialog; and `sign.sh` takes the identity wherever it finds it. Ad hoc is what a build gets if the identity was taken out again, as the script advises when that signature fails, or was never made. What anybody did after the third refusal is not known. *Three, known* (a-permission-belongs-to-a-signature): to macOS each ad-hoc build is a new app; the permission is gone, and the old build's entry under Accessibility still looks switched on. The last lines of `make install` do say that Arbor waits, and that the entry may belong to another signature. *Four and five, seen on hosted Macs in that state, with posted keys*, as above: Arbor waits and holds no key, which is `Controller.activeBindings` without the permission, and ⌃⌥A reaches the app in front. *Not shown*: that this is what happened in that session. The scripts are the first build's, file for file. A case on the first link is on its way, with its cure. What shows, by the runs' pictures: the item is a warning triangle in each of these three states; in the first probe's two waiting states the welcome window is open besides; after the permission was taken away nothing else is on the screen. **The other candidate has Arbor running** (with-fns-flag-on-the-event-arbors-letter-keys-are-not-arbors). Two more roads fit a running Arbor: the app's own hot key on the same chord (macos-never-refused-a-shortcut-that-another-process-holds), and a key put in further in than the keyboard (macos-takes-a-hot-key-away-between-the-session-and-the-annotated-session). To hold no key in these states is what the specs ask (F63, criterion 5: "with none, no shortcut"; F40; F41). What no spec weighed is that the habit outlives the state: the same fingers reach the app. Ruled (Q29): ⌃⌥A is never bound again, and a key of Arbor's that is not Arbor's at that moment is something Arbor knows and says. No detector of the gate has an eye for it.

Then a second probe that is not on the trunk yet, by another session, one run on a hosted Mac (macOS 26.6.2) on the first build itself, its commit and the probe and nothing else: an app in front and a listener in the background with ears of every kind, taps at three points, monitors, a menu, a view, and Arbor's own log counted line by line. entries.expected: A key registered a second time, with Carbon's bit for fn, is a second key: a press fires the one registration or the other, whatever the key.
entries.happened: For a letter, a sign, ↩, Space and ⎋ it is: `RegisterEventHotKey` with 1 << 17 answers 0; a press with fn's flag fires that registration once and the app in front gets nothing; a plain press does not fire it; both held by one process, neither is refused and each press fires its own. **For arrows, F5, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down and forward delete, which carry the flag by nature, macOS takes the two for one: either alone fires with the flag and not without, and held both ways a press fires both**: down, down, up, up: a command would run twice. Bits it does not know (1 << 16, 1 << 23) it ignores: such a registration behaves as a plain one, so a macOS that does not know 1 << 17 would fire both at every press of every key. The release is reported once, also when fn comes up before the key. The numeric-pad flag changes nothing; nor does `kEventHotKeyExclusive`. **macOS 15 answers as macOS 26 does**: 87 rows in both tables, held against each other by a script, and not one differs. Asked of macOS 15 besides: the key down plainly, fn down, the key up: the release comes under the number that went down, the other is silent, the app gets nothing; a key-down marked as a repeat, with the flag, after fn went down: the other does not fire on it, and it does not reach the app.

entries.expected: What codesign may do with a key in a keychain that a test has made for itself, it may do with one in a person's login keychain. Six roads were tried in such keychains on three releases of macOS, no dialog came on any, and it was written down, and told to four others, that nobody needs to be asked. And a dialog goes when the program that caused it is killed.
entries.happened: In the login keychain an imported key has five access entries, among them `partition_id: apple-tool:`; codesign's partition is `apple:`, so macOS asks: "codesign wants to access key “…” in your keychain. To allow this, enter the “login” keychain password." Always Allow makes the list `apple-tool:, apple:`, and nothing is asked again. In a keychain made with `security create-keychain` in a folder under /tmp the same import gives three entries and no such list, and nothing is asked. A login keychain made anew asks like the old one. **By what has been measured it is where the file lies, not what it is called or who made it** (on macOS 26.6.2 two keychains there, one under a throwaway HOME and one under the account's own, were asked about, and none of those that three scripts made in folders under /tmp): a keychain made the same way as `arbor-f13.keychain-db` in ~/Library/Keychains, of a throwaway HOME at that, is asked about too ("enter the “arbor-f13” keychain password"), on the macOS on which the one under /tmp was not; so is `arbor-road.keychain-db` beside the account's login keychain, and that dialog takes the password the file was made with. This case's name says less than that. After Deny codesign says `errSecInternalComponent` and the dialog goes at once; a dialog that nobody answers outlives codesign (twenty seconds of twenty, after TERM and after INT) and the key it asks about, until Deny or Escape: six minutes on it was still there, over Gatekeeper's own dialog about a download. An unlocked keychain takes any password on macOS 14 and 15; 26 looks at it (exit code 51), and refuses, for a file named login.keychain-db, the very password it was made with, in its dialog too.

Where the file lies: `scripts/mac-shell/check-F13-system.sh` on 26.6.2 the same day, five of whose six failures followed from that dialog.

entries.happened: In 82 menu bars on hosted Macs (macOS 26.6.2; 5,384 rows, each distinct in its app): **a fifth bit, 16, is fn (the Globe key)**, in 1,445 rows; all but one of the menu bars have it, from macOS's own Window → Move & Resize, which writes fn⌃← as 28 with the arrow's own code 123 and not as Home. **A letter comes in capitals whatever ⇧ says.** **What ⇧ makes of a key comes either way**: as the sign that is typed, and then never with the bit for ⇧ (⌃⌥: is 14 with `:`, ⌘* is 0 with `*`; 161 rows), or as the key's plain character with the bit (72 rows in 26 apps, 29 of the 30 digits among them); one app has ⌘+ and ⇧⌘= side by side. Arrows, ↩, Space, ⎋, ⇥, ⌫ and the paging keys have a virtual key, with or without a character beside it; a letter, digit or sign never has one. **One item shows the glyph of Clear and gives virtual key 53, which is ⎋**, not 71. A first reading of the numbers that went by the header took fn⌃⌥⇧← for ⌃⌥⇧←, and lost ⌘* on a layout that says nothing about ⇧. **An app goes on building its menu bar after it has one**: of two runs one read 39 shortcuts in an app and the other 50, one 58 and the other none, and a large editor gave 5 of its 121. **And the three large browsers had none at all, in two runs, for another reason than the slowness it was first put down to**: the hosted image installs them from the package manager with the quarantine mark on, so macOS asks whether an app downloaded from the internet may be opened, and nobody is there to answer; the picture shows the three questions stacked.

Accessibility gives the rows below the cut the places they would have had, and a press there closes the menu and chooses nothing. For a person on a small display Pause and Quit are below the fold (the board, 1.26).

entries.copes: MenuModel.tallest: Arbor's menu is at most 600 points high in every state, so nothing of it is cut off on a display 768 high (docs/MENU.md, rule 3). The suite's helper still scrolls a menu that is cut off to its end before it presses.

entries.expected: A row of a menu is 22 points high, as on earlier systems and in the fake Mac; 29 rows and four headings "just fit a 13-inch display".
entries.happened: macOS 26 gives a row 24 points, a heading 24, a separator 11, and 5 above and below. Arbor's menu was 822 points high; a display 768 high shows 668 of a menu, between the menu bar and the Dock, and scrolls the rest. Pause Arbor and Quit Arbor were below the fold, and Accessibility went on giving them the places they would have had, off the display.

The sizes were first read off a picture of the open menu, which gave the row and the sums but split them a point wrong (12, 23, 6); then `NSMenu` was asked, in a test, and its sizes put Quit Arbor at 836 exactly.

entries.expected: The notice that the screen parameters changed, which becomes `displaysChanged`, means that a display came, went or changed, and one change is one notice. The fake's minimize sends one change of the window.
entries.happened: macOS posts it at every minimize and restore, 15 to 20 ms after "miniaturized", because the Dock has grown or shrunk. It posts it several times in a row when a display comes or goes, and for a display that only blinked on wake. A minimize laid out twice and a plug five times. How far apart the notices come has not been measured.

entries.happened: A setFrame that only moves a window which is below its minimum size makes it grow to that size. It is the size that does it. Today's layer sets the place alone where the size stays (`FramePlan.steps`), and in a later comparison a window below its minimum (446×348 for 700×500) kept its size for as long as it was only moved and grew when it was first resized. `FakeWindowSystem.accepted` enforces the minimum at every call, so in the rehearsal it had grown long before.

entries.expected: What an app did to its window just before it hung is known once it wakes.
entries.happened: An app moves its own window 1 ms before it hangs for 5 s. "Resized" and "moved" arrive while it hangs, each read waits a second and fails, and when the app wakes nobody reads the frame again: Arbor goes on believing the old frame, and no `windowChanged` ever comes. At 50 ms before the hang all is well.
entries.found: The real Accessibility layer run on Linux against a model of a Mac (`make mac-on-linux`). On the model only: nobody has seen it on a Mac. A random walk that went on past listed faults met it; its story is in a follow-up that is not on the trunk yet.

entries.expected: A call that got no answer did not happen. In the fake a hung app's window stays where it is, and the app that wakes reports it there.
entries.happened: Measured with a timeout of 1 s: the app carries the queued call out when it wakes. A move out of view that timed out lands late, comes back as a report of the person's own doing, and Arbor remembers the corner as the place the person chose. Measured again on a hosted Mac while Arbor lives: at a pause half a second into a hang, a position and a size sent with a timeout of 0.1 s a call had both windows in view at the script's first look after the app woke, some 18 s later. That it was those calls and not a later try of Arbor's is read from the log, which lacks the line such a try writes; the trunk's run of the same script has that line, 18.6 s after the pause. **But only while the sender lives.** This case used to say that a window goes out of view after Arbor is gone; nobody had seen that, it was an inference written down as a measurement, and a model of a Mac was built on it. Tried since: Arbor quits half a second into the hang, having sent the same calls; 22 s after the hang began both windows are still past the corner, at the size they had there, though the calls named a place and another size. macOS drops what a process asked once that process is dead. Seen of calls with the timeout of 0.1 s only; that the app had woken by then is inferred from the script's other sessions, where the same hang ends in the same second. A call with a longer timeout, and one the app is in the middle of when the sender dies, have not been tried. The stand-ins play none of it.
entries.found: A probe of the Accessibility layer on a real Mac. The consequence was then played headless by moving the fake's window by hand. Later a script that hangs a test app on a hosted Mac, before and after a cure that leaves word with the app at a quit and at a pause; neither is on the trunk yet.
entries.copes: open

entries.expected: A window that has not moved keeps its coordinates, or reports new ones. So a frame Arbor remembers for a floating window stays a place on its display.
entries.happened: Frames are global. When another display becomes the main one (a lid closes or opens, a display is rearranged in System Settings or returns elsewhere) the origin moves. Every window has new numbers, macOS takes the windows along, and apps post nothing. Arbor set floating windows back to their old global frames: with the lid closed a window slid to the right edge until a strip of 2 to 9 % showed, a chance overlap passed for a place somebody chose, and ⌃⌥0 did not fetch it.
entries.found: The silence is stated by the review of the Accessibility layer. The harm was found in a working day with a laptop and an external display, replayed in the simulator; random walks had met it hours earlier. What macOS does here is reasoned, not recorded: every trace has one display, and no real lid has been closed with Arbor running. A script with a virtual display left of, above and right of the main one tries it on hosted Macs.
guards: e2e: move the display to the left of the main one (negative x)
entries.copes: AXWindowSystem.refreshFrames reads every window's frame again before it reports that the displays changed. `followDisplaysThatMoved` shifts what a workspace remembers along with its display's corner, unless the window itself spoke within 30 s.

entries.expected: A window that has been reported as created can be classified at once.
entries.happened: Some apps give new windows their subrole a moment after creating them. Looked at too early they are not standard windows and would be turned away for good.
entries.found: Stated in a comment of the Accessibility layer; no run is named.

The stand-in reported a new window first and gave it the keyboard and the front place afterwards; now it gives both first, and the reports come in the order they came in.

entries.happened: macOS gives a new window the keyboard, so the view goes to it. A new window that a rule docked, and that became a tile, pulled the view onto it.

entries.expected: Ordering a panel in costs what it cost the first time or less, and whatever it costs is the process's own time: the display goes on showing what everybody else draws. Films in which the display showed one picture for up to a second in the middle of a motion were therefore read as a fault of Arbor's: of the stage coming down too early, of handing the keyboard to another app while the stage is up, of a tile's fade.
entries.happened: The first time in a process's life that a panel which draws itself in `draw(_:)` is shown again after seconds out of view, a hosted Mac's display stands still for most of a second. For Arbor that is the first way back to a view with a tile in it, once after every start: 433 to 1,450 ms in 15 of 18 fresh starts filmed over three runs (250, 250 and 134 in the others), with motion and without; the 22 later ways back took 33 to 50 ms, but for one of 134. **A plain tool with no Arbor anywhere gets the same, five times of five**: it shows a panel call for call as `TilePanel.show` does, puts it away for 3.4 s and shows it again: 1,234 and 1,133 ms, and 784, 880 and 900 when it also does to three windows all that Arbor does in that act; once the display stood still for 0.8 s after the tool had ended. It needs nobody to film it: of five such starts with no stream of the display, in three the window list was kept waiting 754 to 800 ms, and in two of those a key that the tool lets go of at once was held for 0.9 s. While a stream runs it is mostly the stream that stops, and the list, the display's beat and the key go on. One sign goes with it every time, in the 18 processes of the third run, Arbor's thirteen and the tool's five: with the act (in Arbor's, 12 to 98 ms after the command, on the system log's one clock) Core Animation sets up drawing through the GPU in that process (`TileView.draw`, `NSViewBackingLayer`, `CABackingStore`, `CA::CG::Queue`, `new_metal_context`, `AppleParavirtGPU`) and logs *Precompiled pipelines disabled on unsupported hardware*. After one of the longest the window server wrote of its own threads *Timer delayed by 1.01s* and *Render::Server callback delayed by 1.04s*, having used next to no processor. Refuted on the way, each by a record: activation (the tool with AXMain, AXRaise and `activate`: 117 ms at most in 18 films; an Arbor that never activates stood still for 1,034 ms; from the Desktop and back the controller asks for no keyboard at all), the fade (later rounds are calm with it), the stage (the same without motion), the order of the starts, and a hold on screen updates (`NSDisableScreenUpdates` does nothing any more: a hold of 1.6 s read 34 ms). Drawing a view again that is in view does not bring it about; nor does a panel out of view for 40 ms, so that two warm-ups after the start, a scratch view and a real tile at a hundredth of its opacity, changed nothing and were taken out again. **Whether a person's Mac does it nobody knows**: the sign names the virtual GPU, and there is no other Mac to ask.
entries.found: Films of a hosted Mac in which each scene was played once on a fresh Mac, so that "the first time" looked like "always in these two scenes". Then three runs on hosted Macs in the night of 2026-10-15 (macOS 26.6.2, VirtualMac2,1): a strip on top of everything whose squares never stop, so that a wait between two frames is a display that stood still also where nothing is meant to move; each act played several times from fresh starts, filmed and unfilmed in turns; the system's log on one clock; and a control without Arbor, which was calm, and proved nothing by it, until it did everything Arbor does.
guards: e2e: the first way out, which costs what macOS makes it cost, took no more than that
e2e: the strip is seen to move, and the display does not stand still by itself
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/check-standstill.sh measures and prints every way back, fails on a later one that stands still for 0.3 s and on a first one over 2.5 s (over 1.5 s it is marked), and has the plain tool's figures beside them, so that a standstill that is Arbor's own would show. Arbor itself does nothing about it. Whoever films or times Arbor on a hosted Mac plays an act once before it counts, and prints what that first play took. A cure that might hold, tried in the plain tool only: draw into a bitmap in memory and hand that over as the layer's contents, so that Core Animation has nothing to draw.

entries.expected: When a listed app steps back and the pause for it ends, Arbor starts again knowing who has the keyboard.
entries.happened: The notice that another app became active is what ends the pause, and `resume` asks `focusedWindow()` inside that same notice. That goes by the app NSWorkspace names as the one in front, which lags the notice by 5 to 50 ms (the-activation-notice-outruns-the-frontmost-app), so the answer can be the old app's window. The cure for the switch of apps looks again; this road does not pass it. Tried since with real apps on a hosted Mac, and it did not show: of 12 such activations every one was named in front at once, and 86 checks in two runs passed on an Arbor without any fix. They came through Launch Services, where the lag has not been seen; it belongs to activations a program asks for.
entries.found: Reading, beside the probe of the switch of apps on hosted Macs; then `check-resume.sh` on a hosted Mac, which did not meet it.
guards: e2e: out of the app Arbor pauses for, to a window the view does not show
e2e: Calculator's window was never taken for the one with the keyboard
entries.copes: scripts/mac-shell/check-resume.sh stands guard and says what it was told. Nothing was changed in Arbor, because nothing was seen to go wrong.

entries.expected: Accessibility, once granted to Arbor, stays granted across builds.
entries.happened: macOS writes down the signature's designated requirement. An ad hoc build's requirement is the hash of that very build, so the next build, or a copy that replaces it, is a stranger: System Settings still shows Arbor switched on, and Arbor is told it has no permission. With the Mac's own certificate it survives: on macOS 26.6.2 a grant made to one build (the requirement names the app and the certificate) held for the next, which was different code, started by macOS and granted nothing. An ad-hoc build installed after that was left waiting, and macOS rewrote the entry to denied (the fourth field 0, the reason 4), so the build with the certificate that followed had to wait as well: one ad-hoc build in between costs the grant. What System Settings shows of such an entry was not looked at.
entries.found: The usability review and the distribution work. `scripts/mac-shell/check-F13-system.sh` on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15.
guards: e2e: their designated requirements are identical
e2e: THE NEXT BUILD, SIGNED WITH THE SAME IDENTITY, RUNS WITHOUT BEING GRANTED ANYTHING
e2e: an ad-hoc build does not inherit the grant
entries.copes: scripts/make-signing-identity.sh and scripts/sign.sh sign every build with a certificate of the Mac's own; Arbor installs no updates for the same reason.

entries.expected: A position call moves a window and leaves its size alone. In the fake the position step of `setFrame` changes the place, and y so that the title bar stays within reach, never the size.
entries.happened: A position call that takes a window to a display whose visible frame is lower than the window cuts its height to that visible height and puts y at the visible top, at once, in that call; the width is left alone. 1000×650 sent to −788,43 came to −788,31 1000×569, sent to −800,31 the same (an 800×600 display to the left); to 12,1123 and to 0,1111 it came to y 1111, 1000×520 (the display below, with the Dock); 798×650 to 12,1111 798×520. 5 calls of 5. The reports are AXResized alone, no AXMoved. 1000 wide on a display of 800 stays 1000. A window that fits (567 high into 569) is not touched. Position, then size ends wrong after it (y 12 too high). **Not tried:** a window too tall sent to a display at the right, one that is only too wide, a smaller display above.
entries.found: A probe that makes the calls one by one through Accessibility, Arbor not running, and reads the frame back after each: one hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2, scale 1, one run of 844 calls and 466 journeys, every line kept and the counts made again from the lines for this page. The second display virtual, 800×600, to the left and below; the test window only.
entries.copes: FramePlan.full sets the size before the position, so a window is small enough before it goes: every order that shrinks first avoided the cut, 9 journeys of 9. Its comment said so without a run and has one now. What becomes of a window that is only moved, at a size believed right (FramePlan.steps), nobody has looked at.

entries.expected: A press is judged by where the button went down.
entries.happened: Since Arbor stands aside where macOS tiles, a mouse-down is taken at the event's own place, and the window under it is looked for in the window server's list as it is when the event is served. Heard 500 ms late in a drag of a second, the window has been dragged away from under that point: no window, no `dragBegan`, six reports that a window changed. Before, place and list were both of the moment of serving and agreed, and the drag began at 551 ms. At 0, 20 and 100 ms late it is still seen. A sibling since: two-cures-that-each-pass-alone-lose-a-drag-together. A cure of three lines, in which the second try skips the rule for swept windows, is judged green on the model and is to land after one run on a hosted Mac.
entries.found: The real Accessibility layer run on Linux against a model of a Mac (`make mac-on-linux`). On the model only: nobody has seen it on a Mac. Its stories are red and listed as known failures: the run demands that the lines go when a cure lands, and from then on they guard it.

entries.expected: Once the permission's rows in the database say allowed and the daemon has been restarted, a waiting Arbor hears yes within seconds.
entries.happened: A process that was started without the permission went on hearing no from `AXIsProcessTrusted()` for 153 s after the rows were set to allowed and the daemon restarted five times, while a new process had the permission at once. Explained since: the script's grant announced nothing. A running process learns of a grant only through one distributed notification (nothing-announces-a-change-of-permission); with it posted, the same waiting Arbor was granted 127 ms later. Arbor's wait for the permission logs nothing, so no log can tell "asked and was told no" from "never asked". Mended, `check-F63.sh` writes, restarts the daemon, waits and posts the notification itself: 30 of 31 at its second run and 32 of 32 at its third (f63-nothing-has-been-pressed-while-the-permission-is-gone).
entries.found: The first run of four Mac shell scripts as they stand, on one hosted Mac, on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `8aa9e10`, macOS 26.6.2, posted events, once). `check-F63.sh`: 15 passed, 16 failed, all behind this. The explanation: probes that are not on the trunk yet, on hosted Macs in the night of 2026-10-15 (macOS 26.6.2, posted events, a debug build).
guards: e2e: it starts by itself when the permission arrives

entries.expected: Quit brings every window into view on the displays that are there.
entries.happened: Arbor hears of a change of displays 1.65 s after macOS says it. A virtual display removed and `quit` 0.3 to 1.4 s later: Arbor says "all windows returned to view", and windows that had been on that display are partly off the display that is left, under 90 % on screen 5 s later, though Accessibility had reported them back on it before the quit. Seen on the code before the cure for late drags and after it. The product owner rules it a fault, of the first severity though narrow in time: a laptop pulled off its dock and shut down is no haste; and "all windows returned to view", said of a window that is not, is a second fault in it. The cause, read and reproduced on Linux beside a control: at a quit the frames are given back by the displays Arbor believes in. Ways back, played: Arbor started again fetches the windows; the display plugged in again has them. **Cured since** (board 1.54). `shutdown`, the road of Quit and of a pause, reads the displays first if one that Arbor believes in is gone, is elsewhere or has another size. It brings its books up to date, moves nothing by that, and lets go by the displays that are, each window once. **Tried on real recordings beside a control**, by the cure's author; the recordings are not on the trunk yet. The test that tries every way back from every state of a trace, played over traces of a virtual display on a hosted Mac: with the cure's two calls taken out, 94 states leave a window out of view, 47 by `quit` and 47 by `float-all`, in the same five traces with the same counts; with them, none by `quit`. In its author's words: a trace cut between macOS's own moves and `displaysChanged` is the state in which letting go goes wrong. The 47 by `float-all` stand (float-all-inside-arbors-wait-for-the-displays-goes-by-the-old-ones). That a Mac has run the cure has not been reported.

Not while there is no display at all; a display that has only just come takes nothing away. Float All is refused meanwhile (float-all-inside-arbors-wait-for-the-displays-goes-by-the-old-ones).

entries.expected: Giving a window the keyboard, or raising it, does nothing to a window that is minimized. The stand-in gave the keyboard to a window that stayed in the Dock, and minimized a window whatever was asked of it meanwhile.
entries.happened: AXRaise fetches a minimized window out of the Dock, one that has only just landed (16 of 16) and one at rest there (4 of 4), and the call takes as long as the flight out: 0.53 to 0.58 s. Making it the main window does nothing to it (8 of 8). Between the naming of the app's next window and the report of the minimizing, 0 to 32 ms, a raise also holds that report back, and the sibling's "main window changed" with it: "miniaturized" and "deminiaturized" then come within a millisecond of each other when the window is out again, and whoever looks at it finds it not minimized. On a held view Arbor sent the keyboard back to the window that was shown as soon as another was named: minimized in front of an audience, it flew to the Dock and straight back, and seven checks of "held and empty" were green over a view that had never been empty. The trace of that was first read as macOS naming the next window half a second early. It was Arbor's own raise that took the half second: a trace with Arbor running shows what macOS does to Arbor's doings, and what macOS does by itself takes a round without Arbor.
entries.found: The first run of the hold's checks on a hosted Mac, by reading its trace behind the green checks; then a probe of macOS alone, no Arbor running: 64 rounds on a hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2, posted events, the app in front, two windows each of the test app and TextEdit, by ⌘M, the yellow button and Accessibility, with Reduce Motion on and off. With the stand-in made true and nothing else changed, five tests of the hold turned red by themselves.

entries.copes: Controller.sendTheKeyboard, for a window that Arbor picks by itself, and Controller.raiseIfItIsThere ask the window first where it is (WindowSystem.whereabouts, a read of AXMinimized that was answered yes in 0 to 2 ms, 20 of 20) and leave alone one that says it is minimized or is gone: it stayed in the Dock 16 of 16. One whose app does not answer is not sent the keyboard either, and a window kept in view is looked at again once a second until its app wakes. Whoever names a window gets it, unasked: Go to…, reveal, zoom and focus with a window's number fetch it out of the Dock, since what a person asks for last counts; and of an app found hanging a question would be the call that times out, after which the layer sends that app nothing. The walks' net minimize-undone speaks whenever a window that has just been minimized is not.

entries.expected: A tapped shortcut is a press and a release with nothing between them. `World.pressKey` lets go at once, before `FakeWindowSystem` delivers anything.
entries.happened: A real key stays down for some hundredths of a second, so the echoes and the focus reports of what the press did arrive before its release. In the comparison every shortcut's reports came in another order. In one recording: the press at 7.599 s, the reports from 7.639 to 7.641, the release at 7.760. `World.pressKey` now delivers what is queued before it lets go, which took eight of the ten differences of order in that comparison; what timers do within that tenth of a second is not played.

entries.expected: A call that fails means that the app did not answer.
entries.happened: With the permission gone every call is taken to answer `apiDisabled`, in the middle of a layout. That is not the app's silence, and the calls to come would be refused as well. Whether calls fail at once on a Mac has never been seen. The stand-in answered a refused `setFrame` with the frame asked for and listed no windows, where today's layer answers nil and goes on giving what it remembers. It does as the layer does now; no test fell.

entries.expected: Every press of the mouse is followed by a release that Arbor's monitor sees, so every drag ends.
entries.happened: Another tool's event tap can swallow the release, or it goes to a window of Arbor's own. The window would stay in the hand for ever: the drop preview stays on screen and Arbor stops following the focus. The band of a rectangle stays likewise. A second press without a release proves the same. For long no run showed a release that was lost: in 674 distinct traces of hosted Macs 2,237 plain presses were heard and not one lacked its mouse-up before the next press (the ledger's keeper's count); the traces showed the opposite, a mouse-up that arrives twice. **Then once:** in the five journeys on the trunk on 2026-10-15 a posted drag of a window's right edge: mouse-down at 9.2071, `resizeBegan` at 9.5222, and no mouse-up. `isMouseButtonDown()` answered true in all 74 askings from 9.68 to 17.15; at 14.1192 the next step's mouse-down came, at 14.1208 `resizeEnded`, and at 17.2398 that step's mouse-up. The pointer tool printed no error. So about 1 in 2,250, and the cause is open: macOS, the runner, or the tool, which had been changed that night. In 54 presses of four later runs each had its release. **How Arbor bore it:** it held the resize open until the next press and took that press for the end of the resize, not for the start of a drag, so the window of that drag was carried over another and stayed floating. Nothing jumped. The watch below could not help: it waits for the button to read as up, and the button read as down.
entries.found: The review of the Accessibility layer, by reading. The cure has only been played by the stand-ins. The one sighting: the trace `pointer` of a run of `make reality` on a hosted Mac (macOS 26.6.2, the trunk at cd3b2dec), read for this page and not in the tree.

So the replayed Arbor "corrected" every window: six divergences in strict mode, none of them Arbor's. A mend of seven lines in the replayer is on its way.

entries.expected: Nobody knew what a size call does to a window that a hand holds, so `setFrame` is kept from a window that is being dragged, and a window pulled out of its slot keeps the slot's size until it is let go. The stand-ins have nothing to say of it.
entries.happened: A size call through Accessibility, made while a drag by the title bar is under way, is taken as at rest; the origin stays; the drag goes on. 63 size calls with the button down (45 on the test window, 15 on TextEdit, 3 on Safari): each took what the same call takes at rest. One AXResized and no AXMoved for each call that changed anything (58 of 58; five more, made at the Dock's line, changed nothing and brought no report), as the call returns (0.7 to 2.1 ms on the test window). The origin moved by 0,0 in all. Afterwards the window follows the pointer as before, never more than a step behind, with the hold it had to a point, and the release is a release: nothing tiles, nothing jumps (35 trials of 35, TextEdit 12 of 12, Safari 2 of 2). **Narrower than where it is held:** 936 wide, held 800 points in, asked 304: the pointer is 496 points to the right of the window's right edge, over nothing of it, and the window still follows at that distance: 5 of 5, TextEdit 3 of 3. The window server keeps the offset the drag began with, not the point under the pointer. **Wider and higher**, held left, in the middle and right: whole, 15 of 15, TextEdit 3 of 3. **The cut in the hand is the cut at rest:** top at 404, asked 600 high, took 300, foot 704 of a visible 705 (5 of 5; TextEdit 3 of 3 and Safari once: 707 of 708); carried up to y 80 the second call is taken whole, still in the hand. **After the release**, 5, 20 and 50 ms after the button was seen up: whole, 15 of 15, TextEdit at 20 ms 3 of 3. **A synthetic pointer stands for a hand**, at rest while the call is made. **Not shown:** a position call in the hand, which a window made narrower would need; a pointer that moves during the call; a modifier held; near an edge or a corner, or with macOS's tile on offer; Arbor's taps in the way; a second display; the Dock at a side; Terminal; Safari beyond three calls.
entries.found: A probe with a synthetic pointer, Arbor not running: one hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, the Dock at the bottom, Reduce Motion on, one run: the test window in eleven kinds of trial five times each, TextEdit in six kinds three times, Safari in two true drags. Every call, reading and report is kept; the repeats were read again from the lines for this page, the counts over all trials are its keeper's.

entries.expected: A window that has been moved to another display is judged by that display from then on: the last call of `FramePlan.full` "applies the size the destination allows". In the fake each step of `setFrame` goes by the display the window's corner is on when the step is made.
entries.happened: For some milliseconds after a position call has taken a window to another display, a size call is still judged by the display it came from. Asked call by call, Arbor not running: from a slot on a virtual display of 800×600 to 12,43 1000×650 on the main one of 1920×1080, the last call always "size 1000×650" at 12,43: it took 1000×557 with the small display to the right or the left (bottom 600, the old display's) and 788×650 with it below (right edge 800, the old display's). By the old display in 10 calls of the 10 that can tell, 0.5 to 5.6 ms after the position call. All four orders of the calls that were tried end short, 12 journeys of 12, size, position, size among them, and it stays so: the same at rest 350 ms later. Nothing in the reports tells: AXMoved comes within 1 to 4 ms. Shrinking is held back too (asked 776 wide, took 812: 24 points stay on the display it came from). From 200 ms on the new display judges, 4 sightings of 4. Where between 6 and 200 ms it turns was not seen. **With Arbor on a Mac, once:** `move-to-display next` of a window docked on a second display of 1280×720, back to the main one of 1920×1080: asked 1443,43 465×947, took 465×677 (720 − 43, the foot of the display it came from); asked again 1 ms later, 677 again; 0.4 ms after that Arbor asks 1443,178 465×677: the window centred in its slot, as for one that will not grow. It stayed so until the quit. The way from large to small was taken as asked. **On a model of a Mac** under the real layer and controller, in a round that is not on the trunk yet, ten stories are its measure: the small display to the right, to the left and below, short three seconds later and ten seconds after that, also on the parent of the change that brought the short window, so it is older than that night; on the trunk it comes right there once the view has been away and back. All ten go by a call of Arbor's own, nine of them by `move-to-display next`. **How often on Macs**, as told by the ledger's keeper: ten calls across displays in 35 traces with two displays, three of them asked to grow: one short, the command above, and two whole. **Ranked by the product owner:** severity 2; wanted before a build is cut, and does not hold it. **Not measured, and so not played:** a drop by hand the moment the window has crossed to the other display; a probe is being written. **Not shown:** an unplugging, or a display that comes back: macos-puts-windows-back-on-a-display-that-returns speaks against a replug being short, since macOS has moved the windows 1.6 s before Arbor hears. The second display was virtual and the windows test windows, in all of it.
entries.found: A probe that makes the calls one by one through Accessibility, Arbor not running, and reads the frame back after each: one hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2, scale 1, one run of 844 calls and 466 journeys, every line kept and the counts made again from the lines for this page. The second display virtual, to the right, to the left and below. Then: Five journeys of test windows (`make reality`) played four ways on one hosted Mac, each once, posted events, the trunk of the morning of 2026-10-15 with the cure of the short window in it: plain, the Dock at the left, the Dock at the right, a second display. Another session's run; the lines named here were read for this page in the traces it brought back, which are not in the tree. By frames: no picture was taken during a journey.
