entries.expected: A window of which it is not known whether it can be as large as its slot is asked where it stands: its own origin, the slot's size. What it takes is what its app allows, and it is then only moved, at that size, to where that belongs.
entries.happened: The answer is the room below the window, not the app's limit (a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock), and Arbor lays the window out at that size in the middle of its slot. `dock W1 left`: asked 170,220 494×650, took 494×484, then put at 12,126 494×484, in a slot of 12,43 494×650. A window framed: asked 12,374 1000×650, took 1000×330, put at 12,203, where 12,43 1000×650 was meant. It is asked again at every later layout, from higher up, so it grows by steps: one window was 484, 578, 625, 648 and at last 650 high. 25 answers were short of what was asked, in all four journeys that set a frame, in three of them at the very first dock. Seen: the calls, the answers and the places. **Which change brought it:** "a refused size costs nobody a second move", since which a window is asked where it stands. On a Mac only the trunk was played. It was bisected afterwards on Linux, on the model of a Mac under the real Accessibility layer and the real controller, once that model had been given the rule: the change's parent green, the change red, the trunk red, and `dock 101 left` ends at the Mac's own 12,126 494×484. On the model it is wider than docking: of 339 stories 1,378 checks hold on the parent and 1,353 on the change; among those that fall are a docked window minimized and restored, an app hidden and shown again, full screen entered and left, a window let go beside macOS's own tiling, and an app that hangs. None of these was seen on a Mac, and that round of the model is not on the trunk yet. Every test and rehearsal on Linux was green, because the stand-ins let a window grow off the screen. **Ruled by the product owner:** severity 1 for a build. An answer clipped by the screen is no refusal. The question where it stands is for a window asked to be smaller; one asked to be larger is moved first, then sized.
entries.found: Five journeys of test windows, played on a hosted Mac and in a rehearsal on Linux and compared line by line (`make reality`): one run (macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, visible frame 0,31 1024×674, the Dock at the bottom, the trunk's Arbor of the night of 2026-10-15), 182 `setFrame` calls, every one read. The traces are kept in collab/evidence/how-far-a-window-grows/first-catch. Found 43 minutes after the change had landed.
entries.copes: Controller.question asks each side of a window in view only to shrink where it stands: nobody in view is asked to grow there, and a window grows in its slot, with one setFrame. Out of view and off the display on both sides it is still asked for the whole size; a low window whose foot lies in the Dock's strip there is not, for nothing grows in it. A short answer that ends on the line of where the window stood (Controller.mayHaveBeenStoppedByTheScreen: an app that carries out a move late) is no refusal: nothing is learnt from it and Controller.place asks once more in the slot. **Seen cured on a Mac**, the same five journeys on hosted Macs, counted with scripts/reality-clip.py and scripts/reality-slots.py: answers cut at the Dock's line 23 without the cure and 0 with it; looks at a docked window on screen that did not fill its slot 30 of 82 and 0 of 82; `setFrame` calls 182 and 155. The control of the same night is told by whoever ran it (its folder has been overwritten since); two other runs without the cure, the first catch and a change of the calls' order alone, were counted again for this page and give the same 23 and 30 of 82. A second witness: the real-window suite on two hosted Macs with the cure, "windows match Arbor's layout" 203 of 203, "in its slot" 27 of 27, "fills the screen" 70 of 70. On the trunk itself after it had landed: 0 cut, and 6 of 77 looks not filling, of which five are a window under macOS's own zoom, which is let be, and one belongs to a-release-can-be-lost. With the Dock at the left, at the right and with a second display: 0 cut, and nothing short but the zoom and a-size-call-right-after-a-change-of-display-is-judged-by-the-old-display. Not shown: real apps.

entries.expected: Position, then size, gives a window its frame. In the fake `setFrame` is one step: size and place change together, and one echo carries the frame asked for.
entries.happened: The size a window may take depends on where it stands. Asked for 12,43 1000×319 from 272,31 480×348, the window first reports 752×319, which is what fits between x 272 and the display's right edge, then moves, then takes 1000. Going back to a floating size it reports 512×661 before 512×673. One command, three reports with three different frames. A large window is clamped in the same way on its way to a smaller display, and the frame Arbor believes a window has can be out of date. The stand-in plays the number of reports this makes (a third where the size does not fit at the old place; none for a window at its minimum, or one that hung over that edge already), not the frames in between, which the real layer does not pass on either: it reads the frame when a report arrives. The whole rule has been read off a later run (a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock): it holds growth back and nothing else, at the Dock as at the right edge. **Across displays the premise was wrong:** that a size cut to what fits at the old place is applied in full at the new one holds on one display; after a change of display the last size call is still judged by the old one (a-size-call-right-after-a-change-of-display-is-judged-by-the-old-display). This case stood here as not played by the stand-ins when a change landed that leant on the stand-ins for it (a-size-clipped-by-the-screen-was-taken-for-the-apps-refusal).
entries.found: A watcher of raw Accessibility notifications that ran beside probe scripts on a hosted Mac. The clamp between displays was seen in a probe of four orders of calls on a hosted Mac (466 journeys, Arbor not running), whose numbers stand in the frame plan's comments (a-position-call-cuts-the-height-of-a-window-taller-than-the-display-it-is-sent-to; collab/reports/2026-10-15-how-far-a-window-grows.md).
entries.copes: FramePlan sizes first what shrinks, then moves, and sizes last what grows, so a window whose frame is known, and whose app moves it at once, grows where it ends up; a window of which no frame is known gets size, position, size, and so does one that grows into a frame that hangs over its display's edge, where growth would be cut. EchoFilter takes the stages in between for echoes. The frame is read back (FramePlan.makingUp): if the size was never asked for and is not right the full plan follows; if it was asked for before the move only and the window is smaller than asked, it is asked once more where the window is by then. For an app that moves late the size still arrives at the old place and is cut there: an answer that ends on such a line may be the screen's and not the window's, so `place` asks once more (Controller.mayHaveBeenStoppedByTheScreen). FramePlan.wasCutWhereItStood is the same fact as a pure function, with the answers measured on a Mac as its tests; nobody calls it yet, and one of the two is to go under the other.

entries.expected: When a focus report (`windowFocused`) arrives, Arbor knows which windows show. A switch of Spaces is one report with its windows.
entries.happened: Switching Spaces brings an app forward before or after Arbor has learnt which windows show now, and the switch itself reaches the controller window by window: those that left, then those that came. With the layout still describing the Space being left, the view stepped out, and a trip to another Space and back lost the zoom. In which order the activation and the Space change arrive has never been measured.
entries.found: Foreseen while Go to… was built, and stated in the Accessibility layer's comments and the architecture notes. No committed trace holds a Space switch.

entries.expected: The frame read back after a move is where the window is, so it can be booked as where Arbor put it.
entries.happened: On a model of a Mac only. An app says yes at once and carries the move out later; a read in between gets the old frame. `AXWindowSystem.setFrame` books that stale frame as where Arbor put the window, so the look 0.3 s later finds the window "strayed" to the very place Arbor sent it, and reports Arbor's own move as the person's ("did not stay where it was put"). Docked windows come right. A floating window comes back moved and shrunk, (624,218 400×300) to (624,405 341×300), and a parked one can be taken for put in the corner by hand. The manner was seen of one app, Safari leaving full screen; that apps have it in general is a guess. A cure to consider: `EchoFilter.hasStrayed` against the frame that was asked for, not the one read back. **Looked for on a Mac since, and not seen:** one call, the frame read back at once and at three later looks (in truth 62 to 209, 200 to 346 and 601 to 757 ms after it), of ten of Apple's apps, one Java app and the test window, Arbor not running: Accessibility's frame at once is its frame at all three looks, 170 results of 170. No app sized at once and moved late, none animates. Nothing is known of the first 60 ms but the reading at once; every app was in the background; no Chromium, Gecko, Electron or Qt.

entries.expected: An event tap stays on, and if macOS switches it off for being too slow the callback hears of it at once.
entries.happened: macOS 26 tells the callback only in place of the next event the tap would have had. So the first gesture after a stall is lost, and a word that finds the tap on is about a switch-off already mended. The check that runs every second is often first, and one freeze could count twice, so that Arbor let go of its taps sooner than meant. Each switch-on while the cause lasts buys another freeze of all input.

entries.expected: An event tap only listens, so it can run on the main run loop like the rest of Arbor.
entries.happened: macOS holds back every tapped event, for every app, until the tap's callback returns. On the main thread, where one Accessibility call can take a second, every click, drag and pinch on the Mac waited with it. With a healthy tap on a thread of its own a mouse-down takes about 0.2 ms longer to reach its app (0.23 ms without Arbor, 0.41 ms with), and one that needs the window list about 3 ms. Those figures are of one click at a time on a quiet Mac. What streams of events cost: every-event-takes-longer-with-arbor-running.

entries.expected: While a process with an active tap does not answer, macOS holds the events the tap has asked for, gives up after a while and passes them on late.
entries.happened: A tapper that hangs costs the Mac one second, and macOS mends it by itself. With nothing taken from anybody and the whole of Arbor halted (SIGSTOP), under full traffic: one hole of 1,071 ms, and 1,154 in a second round, in which 101 and 111 events of all kinds were lost, not late. Then macOS's own timeout had switched the mouse-down tap off (the window server's list says so), and everything arrived again with the process still halted. Halting the whole process flatters: if only the thread that keeps the clock sleeps while the taps' thread goes on answering, nothing times out.

entries.expected: The messaging timeout set on an app's element holds for its windows' elements, and one set on any element applies to that element. Without one of their own, elements keep the system's default of 6 s.
entries.happened: A timeout belongs to one element object, and window elements do not go by their app element's. Measured: window elements without a timeout of their own took 1.55 s a call, not 6. Set on the system-wide element it becomes the whole process's and covers every element, those made on the fly included. A timeout of 0 means the default of six seconds, not "do not wait".

entries.expected: A window takes the size it is given unless its app refuses. In the stand-ins `FakeWindowSystem.setFrame` takes any size anywhere, and so does the fake Mac: a window may grow off the bottom of the screen.
entries.happened: A size call that makes a window grow stops where its bottom edge comes to the visible frame's bottom less 1, and its right edge to the display's right edge. The origin stays. With the visible bottom at 705 the bottom came to 704 in 23 answers of 23 (stood and asked 170,220: 494×650 asked, 494×484 taken; 12,374: 1000×650 asked, 1000×330 taken); the right edge to 1024 in 2 of 2 (687,106: 494 wide asked, 337 taken). **Growth only.** It never made a window smaller: one that stood with its bottom at 704 already kept its height (asked 273×650, took 273×348). An edge that is off the display is free: a parked window at 1023,677 took 1000×650 whole, 2 of 2 (one that is only past the line is not: an-edge-in-the-docks-strip-is-held-and-only-one-off-the-display-is-free). Position calls are not touched: a window that got its whole size in the corner was then put at 687,106 325×650, its bottom at 756, 51 points behind the Dock, until Arbor's next move. **It is decided where the window stands when each size call arrives**, not by whether the request names a new place. One `setFrame` of Arbor's is up to three calls, size, position, size: moved into a slot a window is clipped at the first and made good at the third, which is why nothing showed for as long as windows were sized on their way (a-size-set-at-the-old-place-is-cut-to-what-fits-there had seen that much). **It is the Dock as it is at that moment**, whatever Arbor has been told: after a window had gone into the Dock an answer stopped at 706, 0.33 s before Arbor heard that the visible bottom was 707. The app's own smallest size wins over it (in an older run: asked 446×348, took 700×500, bottom 720, right edge 1278). The point less belongs to the Dock, not to the bottom (growth-stops-a-point-short-only-on-the-side-where-the-dock-is; at the right: with-the-dock-at-the-right-a-growing-window-stops-a-point-short-of-it). A window cannot grow into a frame that hangs over an edge once it stands there (a-window-cannot-grow-into-a-frame-that-hangs-over-an-edge-once-it-is-there), and what that cost Arbor is a-window-let-go-low-lost-its-own-size. **Real apps are cut alike:** asked call by call, Arbor not running, taller than there is room, the bottom came to the visible bottom less 1 in TextEdit, Finder, Safari, Java's jconsole, Preview, Script Editor, Activity Monitor, Console, Notes and (its cells happened to fit) Terminal: 10 apps of the 10 that could be judged, of 11 tried; Calendar's least height put its foot in the Dock's strip. Wider than the display: right edge 1024 in TextEdit, Finder, Safari, Java; Terminal 1026, which rounds to cells after the cut. With a neighbour a window is cut at the edge of its own display, not of the desktop; one that lies across the shared edge with the larger part on the neighbour grows to the neighbour's far edge (one sighting): the larger part decides, where ScreenLines' users go by the corner. **Not seen:** call by call, more than one Mac and one macOS; Chromium, Gecko, Electron, Qt (two browsers did not open); a Retina display; a window in front. Whether AppKit or the window server does it is not known; by reading it leans to AppKit in the app's process.
entries.found: Five journeys of test windows, played on a hosted Mac and in a rehearsal on Linux and compared line by line (`make reality`): one run (macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, visible frame 0,31 1024×674, the Dock at the bottom, the trunk's Arbor of the night of 2026-10-15), 182 `setFrame` calls, every one read. The traces are kept in collab/evidence/how-far-a-window-grows/first-catch; and 313 calls of two older runs. Then asked of macOS call by call, Arbor not running (844 plain calls on one hosted Mac that set AXSize and AXPosition, the frame read back after each; the Dock at the bottom, at the left and hidden; 1024×768 alone and 1920×1080 with a second display on three sides), of a test window and of eleven real apps, ten of Apple's and one in Java: collab/reports/2026-10-15-how-far-a-window-grows.md.
entries.copes: FramePlan moves first what grows, so a window grows where it ends up; one that grows into a frame that hangs over its display's edge gets size, position, size, and takes along what it got where it stood. The controller asks nobody in view to grow where it stands (a-size-clipped-by-the-screen-was-taken-for-the-apps-refusal), and gives a frame that hangs over a line through Controller.give (a-window-let-go-low-lost-its-own-size). ScreenLines is the one model of the rule, for the controller, the fake and the nets: the fake plays the plan's calls one by one, the point short of a Dock below and at the right, each edge by itself, and an edge that is free only off the display (in the strip of a Dock at the right that is a guess by likeness). That a size call right after a journey to another display is judged by the display the window came from it does not play yet.

entries.happened: The other four are one journey in four circumstances: into a frame that hangs over the right edge by a point (530,43 495×400 on a display 1024 wide; 1426,43 on 1920). Position, then size ends 494 wide; size, position, size whole: 4 of 4 (the Dock at the bottom, at the left, hidden; 1920×1080). A window cannot grow into such a frame once it has been moved there; the old order sizes it where it stood, where there was room, and a window that is moved afterwards is not cut again. Only 1 point, only the right edge and only a start with room were tried. For slots inside the visible frame it never matters. It matters for whatever `setFrame` is asked to hang over an edge: a floating window given its own size back low on the display, a window on its way out of view.

entries.happened: Let go low on the display, its own height does not fit between its title bar and the Dock, and a window cannot grow into a frame that hangs over that line once it stands there (a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock). A window of 400×600 out of a slot 319 high, let go at 624,404, kept 400×319: its bottom was in the Dock's strip already, where nothing grows. Arbor wrote 400×319 down as the window's own size, and docked and floated again that is what it got, for good. The slot had no room for 600 either, so the first of the three calls a frame is set with could not help. The same with every frame that hangs over the bottom or the right edge and is given back from a slot with no room for it. **Seen** on a round of the model of a Mac that is not on the trunk yet (the real Accessibility layer and the real controller; that round plays the rule as the probe of bare calls measured it, the model on the trunk does not), and in the stand-ins once they played it: one seed in a hundred of a random test (815,492 304×544 on a display 900 high, cut to 407). **Not seen on a Mac under Arbor.** **Ruled by the product owner:** a cut size is never written down as a window's own; the window ends at its own size with its title bar where it was let go, hanging over the bottom if that is so: sized where it fits, then moved. One point short at the visible bottom above a Dock is no refusal, and nothing is learnt from it or asked again.
entries.found: The stand-in made true for another fault (a-size-clipped-by-the-screen-was-taken-for-the-apps-refusal) turned one seed of a random test red; then a story told on the model of a Mac. The rule itself: 844 bare Accessibility calls on one hosted Mac, macOS 26.6.2.
entries.copes: Controller.give plays the three calls beforehand (ScreenLines, the one model that the controller, the fake and the nets share): one setFrame wherever that will do, to a point; where it will not, the window is sized straight above or beside where it is going, up against the line (at the top of the visible frame if it fits nowhere), and then only moved, which macOS does not hold back. A cut nobody foresaw shows in an answer that is all macOS allows where the window stands or stood, and is made good the same way, once. What give returns as the window's own keeps the size that was asked for on a side the screen kept short, judged where the window was sized and not where it was taken afterwards. The price: a hop up and back, in that case alone. The two counters of moves on Linux know it by what one request would have made of the frame (FakeWindowSystem.isSizedWhereItFits); scripts/mac-shell/jolts.py, which judges hosted Macs, does not. Seen on a hosted Mac, once (scripts/mac-shell/check-own-size.sh, run 38729336293, 45 checks of 45; macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, the Dock at the bottom, test windows; its output was read for this page and is not in the tree): dragged out of a low slot by the real pointer and let go low it took 400×600 and kept it; left hanging over the bottom at 560,380 400×600 and over the right edge at 504,71 640×300, it was given back whole and where it was by Float All, by a pause and by Quit; as high as the visible frame it came back a point short at most; let be at a start it stood at 84,101 950×400 as before. Not varied: one Mac, one run, the Dock nowhere else, no real app.

entries.happened: A window macOS had tiled or zoomed gets its old size back while it is dragged away by its title bar: a drag during which the size changes. It was taken for an edge resize (`resizeBegan`): no dock, and gaps moved. Measured: the size comes back over about 0.3 s in 17 `AXResized` reports between the `AXMoved` reports of the drag, and each time one point larger both ways (480×348, 481×349, 482×350, 483×351, 484×352 after four tiles).

entries.expected: When a display's corner moves, every remembered frame is shifted once. A report of a window's new place cannot come before the list of displays that Arbor can ask for has changed.
entries.happened: Where a window's own report has brought Arbor's memory up to date before even that list changes, no guard has anything to see, and the frame was shifted a second time. The lid opens, macOS takes a window from 590,429 to 2318,106, and Arbor sent it on to 4046,-217: a fifth of it showing, and ⌃⌥0 did not fetch it. Whether a Mac can produce that order is not measured: the Accessibility observer and AppKit's news of the screens come through different ports of one run loop, whose order of service is not specified. Recorded since, in 17 traces with one virtual display on a hosted Mac: this order was not seen. The screens' word comes first, and AppKit's list is the new one by the time any window speaks. What was seen, and what it means for the controller: macos-moves-windows-at-once-and-arbor-hears-of-the-displays-later. That order decides three faults found in one night: the double shift, a hop, and a strip of 32 points that no key fetches.
entries.found: A random walk in the chaos lab and a replay of a person's day in the simulator, each display story played in both orders. Never seen on a Mac.

entries.expected: Taking the permission away only disables Arbor, and its event taps are harmless until Arbor removes them.
entries.happened: With Arbor's event taps in and the right to tap withdrawn, the first event that matches a tap that is switched on is dropped, and from then until Arbor has removed its taps every event of every kind is dropped, for the whole Mac: clicks, keys, the wheel, also kinds that match no tap that is switched on. Lost, not late. **How often.** The first table, fourteen valid rounds: with nobody running nothing was lost (three rounds); with Arbor and no taps 0 of 3,400 events; with Arbor and its taps events were lost in 9 of 10 rounds, on all three roads: the row deleted and the daemon killed, in silence (95, 15, 5 and 65 events, and 10 of 1,360 key events in an older table); the same, and announced (5, 0); `tccutil reset` (90, 95, 5). Eight more rounds by `tccutil` since: 85, 10, 90, 100, 10, 10, 115, 55. Its holes were 994, 1,046, 126, 955, 218, 1,002, 1,091, 135, 194, 1,248 and 612 ms, the longest a second and the timer's tolerance; the shortest on any road 85. The controls stand at 0 lost in eight rounds with nobody and in three with Arbor without taps. **Under traffic**, on the trunk's Arbor with the gestures asked for (14 rounds, none invalid), by `tccutil`: with the scroll tap on, 4 of 480 key events lost (the taps out after 182 ms) and 0 (95 ms); with the gesture tap, 39 of 717 (a hole of 736 ms) and 54 of 720 (865 ms). At one event a second nothing was lost: 26 of 26 with the scroll tap on (301 ms) and 26 of 26 pinch events (770 ms): Arbor was out before the next event its taps had asked for. **How long.** A hole ends 30 to 100 ms after Arbor's line in the log: its length is the wait for the next tick of `PointerInput.checkPermission`, a timer of one second. Arbor's main thread, looked at every 5 ms from the deed on, was idle in 998 of 1,005, 1,017 of 1,020 and 822 of 834 looks: nothing stalls. After the taps have gone nothing is lost. **Where it begins.** Not at the withdrawal: at the first event that matches a switched-on tap. Sixteen valid rounds on `tccutil`'s road: in all eleven with a loss the first event lost is a mouse-down, and what was posted between the deed and that press arrived, once 772 ms after the deed. Three rounds with Arbor lost nothing, because its tick came first. So whoever only types loses nothing until the next press or gesture. **Nothing stays stuck**, 16 rounds of 16, but each kind goes its own way after an up was lost whose down had arrived. A key is held to be down, by the window server's key state and by the app, for 6.8 to 6.9 s in the probe: it is put right by its own next press and release and by nothing before that, not silence, a move, a notch or a click. A modifier (⇧: key state, flags and AppKit's flags alike) stayed on for 3.2 to 3.4 s, which was the silence: it is put right by the next event of any kind, and not by itself. The button never sticks, its down being the first thing lost; an up without its down was seen nine times, nothing was held, and the next click was whole. No drag goes on: pressed on a title bar, the window stayed when the pointer moved. Nothing stayed stuck after a loss in the middle of a held ⌃⌥-drag with the band showing either, five valid rounds of five, by `tccutil` and by the row and the word (12 checks in the first, nine in each of the others, all passed): no tap left, no band or panel left with the button still down, the release arrived, the next plain click and drag whole, no modifier stuck. Whether a real key's repeat runs on cannot be seen with posted keys. **Two separate things.** The flag turns at the distributed notification; the right to tap is withdrawn by the daemon's own doing (`tccutil`, or a daemon that has read its database again). On the gentlest road, the row deleted and the word given with the daemon left alone, Arbor took its taps out of its own accord within its second and nothing was lost, eight rounds of eight. Then the first loss on that road: 1 gesture event of 720, the taps out 563 ms after the deed; three more rounds of the same run lost nothing (0 of 478, 0 of 720, 0 of 480). The grace is not quite always enough for a clock of one second. It was first read as "macOS had withdrawn nothing", and that is corrected: with a tapper that asks, the flag said no 2 ms after the word and the right went too, 470 to 744 ms after the deed; one that asked nothing lost nothing in 8 s. It seems that asking is what makes the daemon look again. For Arbor the order there is the word, the flag at its next look, and two thirds of a second of grace. **Which question turns.** A bare tapper asked five every 10 ms, seven valid rounds. By `tccutil` the first event is dropped 30 to 46 ms after the deed, and only a trial `tapCreate`, an active tap made and thrown away, turns: no, 0 to 33 ms after the first dropped event. `CGEvent.tapIsEnabled` of its own tap never turns (yes to the end, 12 s on), nor `AXIsProcessTrusted`, `CGPreflightListenEventAccess` or `CGPreflightPostEventAccess`, and in a dense stream the callback is told nothing. One trial costs 254 to 481 µs at the median, 1.5 to 5.3 ms at the 99th percentile, at worst 6 to 24 ms and once 80; the others 0 to 96 µs. **What ends it.** Keys were dropped though Arbor has no tap for keys, and the wheel with its tap switched off: once begun the drop takes everything. But a tap that is in and switched off never starts it, nor one that is on and has no traffic (macos-drops-all-input-behind-any-tap-whose-owner-lost-the-right): switching taps off is enough to keep a lost right harmless while they are off. **What is not known.** A trackpad's touches as the event that starts the drop have not been tried: no hosted Mac has a trackpad. Whether real keys and buttons are dropped as posted ones are, nobody can know from a hosted Mac; nor in which order the word, the flag and the right go at the real switch (the-switch-in-system-settings-asks-a-script-for-a-password). And today, if the thread that keeps Arbor's clock slept at the wrong moment while the taps' thread went on answering, nobody would take the taps out and nothing would time out: every press would cost the Mac about a second (macos-drops-all-input-behind-any-tap-whose-owner-lost-the-right). Halting the whole process flatters, because then macOS mends it (a-tapper-that-hangs-costs-the-mac-a-second-and-macos-mends-it). A last net outside that thread is being asked about. Decided on the board (1.46): in doubt, all taps off. What is tested today is only that the taps go within three seconds. **As Arbor ships nobody meets it**: `Settings.pointerGestures` is false, the one switch that is asked before `gesturesEnabled`, `scrollZoom`, `frameRectangleModifier` and `frameRectangleOnDesktop`, and off it means that Arbor installs no event tap at all, whatever a settings.json of an earlier build says of the four. Whoever switches "Trackpad and mouse gestures" on has the hole.

Until then it was hearsay, quoted in the spec and in the code: "macOS has been reported to stop all input".

entries.expected: A minimize is over when it is asked for, and an app answers Accessibility at any time.
entries.happened: The flight takes 0.50 to 0.66 s from the window server's first change to the app's first word, and 0.50 to 0.91 s from the key, the button or the call (over 0.66 s in 4 of 63 rounds), which leaves little to the second after which Arbor's layer takes an app for hung. For all of it the whole app answers nobody: a read of another window of the app, asked in flight, takes the rest of the flight (474 to 743 ms), polled every 4 ms or every 50 alike. The window server lists the window on screen all the way, its bounds changing from 25 to 90 ms after the hand (three times of 51 later: 93, 158 and 363 ms), then not at all. The box first widens toward the Dock's slot (480 to 712 points) before it shrinks: for a quarter of a second the window server has the window over its neighbour, and whoever reads its list then sees an overlap. Reduce Motion changes none of it. The three notifications, focused window, main window, miniaturized, come when the window has landed, in that order.

Whatever Arbor asks of that app meanwhile for another reason waits on the main thread for up to the rest of the flight, which is under the second after which an app counts as hung.

Front to back it was W5 W4 W1 W3, where W4 is the other app's. The real test app calls `NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps:)` for it. `World.switchTo(app:byItself:)` now plays that: the frontmost of the app's windows gets the keyboard and only that one is raised. ⌘Tab goes on raising all of them.

entries.expected: A switch of apps is one report, the window that has the keyboard now. `FakeWindowSystem.userFocus` sends `windowFocused` and nothing else, `userSwitchesApp` one `keyboardFocusMoved` and no window, and the fake Mac's `World.bringForward` reports nothing of the keyboard.
entries.happened: When an app comes forward or steps back (`AXApplicationDeactivated`, `AXApplicationActivated`, the workspace's notice) the Mac's layer reports `keyboardFocusMoved`, up to three times. On a real switch two of them can reach the controller before `windowFocused`, by up to 50 ms: for that long the controller knows that the keyboard moved and not where to. Counted in the recordings where nobody pressed anything and Arbor had not asked: of 15 changes of app, twice in 10, and in 7 of those as the window, moved, moved; once in 3, never in 1, three times in 1; one of them before the window in 5. Within an app the window alone, 31 of 34. `FakeWindowSystem.userFocus` now plays the most common order, and the fake Mac with it, since `World.giveKeyboard` goes through it. No stand-in plays a "moved" before the window. Counted again by who had the keyboard before. After Arbor's own `focus`: from another window of the same app never (13 of 13); from another app's window twice (9 of 10); from no window that Arbor knows once (11 of 22; never in 9, twice in 2). So it is one word for each app Arbor observes that comes or goes. The fake said it once after `focus` whoever had the keyboard, never for the first window to get it, once when an app hid with nobody to take over (a Mac: twice), and never for an app that comes forward again after Finder. It plays all four now; no test fell.

entries.expected: ⌘Tab to an app that is busy for a moment is followed, by `windowFocused`, as soon as the app answers again.
entries.happened: ⌘Tab, or the app in front quitting, to an app that hangs for two seconds and whose window is out of view: the window stays in its corner with the keyboard in it, for good. The question for the focused window waits out its second and comes back empty like "no focused window". The app is not marked as silent, so nobody asks whether it is back, and the next switch to it waits again: three switches, three seconds of a deaf Arbor. Was it marked already, the report is dropped at once, waking brings a look at its windows and no focus, and "application activated", which it posts on waking, only says that the keyboard moved. On a polite Mac, with no other bad manner; the cure for the lost switch of apps does not reach it.

Its stories are red and listed as known failures: the run demands that the lines go when a cure lands, and from then on they guard it.

entries.expected: A window that was hidden with its app comes back where it lay among the others. `FakeWindowSystem.setHidden` and the fake Mac's `unhide` left the order of windows as it was.
entries.happened: An app that shows again without coming forward (`unhideWithoutActivation`) brings its windows back as one block, in the order they had among themselves. Before the hide the order was W1 W2 W4 W3, W4 being another app's. On one hosted Mac, with Finder in front, they came back as W1 W2 W3 W4; on another, with W4 in use, as W4 W1 W2 W3. So the block lies right behind the window that has the keyboard, or in front of everything if none has. Two runs, one test app: what an app does that comes forward as it shows (a click on its Dock icon) is another matter, and where the block goes when the app in front has several windows has not been seen.

entries.expected: Asking a running app for its icon and drawing it takes a few milliseconds, so a motion can do it while it is being set up, inside `animate`. The stand-in for the overlays has everything at hand at once.
entries.happened: macOS draws an app's icon at a size the first time anybody asks for it at that size, and keeps it, across runs of Arbor. On a hosted Mac that had drawn none, eight apps' icons (24 points for the colour, 256 for the card) took 4.7 s on the main thread, before the stage was up and so before any window moved; `arborctl` gave up on the dock after 5 s. A minute later, in a new run of Arbor, the same eight took 27 ms. Two earlier runs: 1.9 s with nine apps, 2.0 s with two, so much of it is paid with the first icon. A hosted Mac is always one that has not paid; a person's Mac is one at Arbor's first run.

entries.expected: An edge that is past its line already is free, as a parked window showed, which took any size. The fake's `setFrame` gave a window whose foot is below the visible bottom whatever height was asked, until it was given the rule.
entries.happened: An edge is free only when it is off the display; in the Dock's strip it is held as it is. Foot at 704, 705 and 706 with the visible bottom at 705: asked for 100 more, the window kept its height, with no report, all three. Calendar, whose least height put its foot at 729 of a visible 711: asked 650, kept 503. Foot at 900 and 1201, off a display of 768: free. Right edge at 1024: held; at 1025: free. **Each edge is judged by itself:** right edge over the display's and foot above the line, the width is free and the height goes to the line and stops (100 + 604 = 704); foot far past and right edge inside, the height is free and the width stops at 1024. Hanging over the left edge changes nothing. **Not seen:** a foot between 730 and 899, so whether 768 is where it turns.

entries.expected: A key pressed while Arbor cannot answer is lost, or goes to the app in front.
entries.happened: Neither. With Arbor stopped by a signal, nine of its keys were pressed: the taps at the keyboard's end heard them, no app got one, and Arbor's log did not grow. Set going again, its log grew by 23 lines, the commands one after another within 140 ms: `arrange` ("arranged 3 windows; 9 saved views are gone"), `zoom`, `show-all`, `back`, `undo`, `toggle-float`, `find`. macOS keeps a hot key for the process that registered it until that process takes it. By reading, not tried: the same would hold for every long hang of Arbor's main thread, as when it waits for an app that does not answer (a-hung-app-holds-every-call-for-the-whole-timeout): what a person presses again because nothing happens is all carried out when Arbor comes to.

entries.expected: An echo follows its call at once, so a `windowChanged` that comes later and that Arbor did not ask for is the person's or the app's doing.
entries.happened: Echoes usually come 2 to 15 ms after the call, but 0.3 to 0.55 s after it for Finder, Terminal and now and then any window. Taken for the person's, such a report would replace a floating window's own frame with the Desktop's, add steps to the undo history or move the view.

entries.expected: A watch on settings.json sees every save.
entries.happened: Most editors write a new file and move it over the old one. That changes the folder, and a watch on the file alone is left holding a file nobody can see any more. Others (VS Code, nano, `echo >`) write in place, which does not change the folder. `sed -i` replaces, some tools delete the file and make it again, and if the file is a link a delete or a rename is all there is to see.
entries.found: The real-window runner, which saves the file both ways, and a Mac shell script that saves it each way and looks where the window server has a docked window afterwards: 40 of 40 on macOS 26.

entries.expected: The stand-ins answer at once, so a command costs what Arbor's own code costs.
entries.happened: Arbor's own work is tens of microseconds; the rest is waiting for other processes. A call takes 0.1 to 0.6 ms from an idle app, 2 to 5 ms for a resize that changes the size, about 9 ms to focus; in traces a `setFrame` took 1 to 20 ms, and 44 ms (Finder) and 101 ms (TextEdit) the first time. A new panel costs about 3 ms when first shown: stepping out to twelve windows took 45 to 53 ms, 30 to 40 of them for a dozen gap panels. A ⇧ mouse-down over a window was held 2.9 ms instead of 0.4 while the window list was read.
entries.found: `took` in every trace of real windows; a measuring run of scripts/mac-shell/perf.sh on a Mac with twelve real windows.
entries.copes: FramePlan makes one call where one does, panels are kept and handed out again, and the stand-ins count calls instead of time. The real window system does not take the hint of `moveTogether` yet.

entries.expected: Arbor hears of a change of displays 1.5 s after it happens.
entries.happened: The 1.5 s begin anew at every notice. Several come at a plug and a dock negotiates for seconds, so `displaysChanged` can be much later than what apps say of their windows. A first cure that believed a window's report for 2.0 s held to 1.9 s and failed from 2.1 s on in a play with time in it. How long a real plug takes nobody has measured.
entries.found: Reading the Accessibility layer, then a replay in arbor-sim with time between the window's report and the displays'. On no Mac.
entries.copes: Controller.spokenLately: a window that has said within the last thirty seconds where it is, and is there, is not moved again with its display's corner.

entries.expected: With a healthy tap on a thread of its own an event takes about 0.2 ms longer to reach its app: the figure of one click at a time.
entries.happened: Measured in streams, on a release build: 18 streams, 17,975 posted events, none lost, three turns of each variant in turns on one hosted Mac of three cores. Median, 99th percentile and worst, in ms. Clicks into a window's content: with no Arbor 0.45, 8.12, 31.9; with Arbor without taps 0.53, 3.70, 6.7; with its taps 2.27, 9.66, 15.0. Presses on a title bar: 0.91, 4.83, 11.2; 1.00, 9.27, 14.2; 3.96, 15.15, 21.9. So the taps' own share is 1.7 to 3.0 ms at the median and 6 at the 99th percentile, and the rest of Arbor costs 0.08 at the median and 4.4 at the 99th on a title bar. Release costs what debug cost (2.27 against 2.46, 3.96 against 3.89, in 24 streams of 23,970 events): the price is the round trip to another process's thread and back, not Arbor's code, and nobody need try to optimise it away. The mouse-down, the only event that passes a tap that is switched on, pays least (0.6 to 0.8 ms); the up, the keys and the wheel's notch of the same beat pay more, because they queue behind it. Over 10 ms late on a title bar were 2, 23 and 142 of about 3,000 (nobody, without taps, with taps): that is where the taps show most. One limit: "without taps" also takes the 52 registered shortcuts out, which errs against the taps.
entries.found: Probes that are not on the trunk yet, on hosted Macs in the night of 2026-10-15 (macOS 26.6.2, posted events), first with a debug build and then with a release build, each with a control on both sides: nobody, and Arbor without taps.
guards: e2e: with Arbor: how long a click on a docked window takes
entries.copes: EventTapThread serves every tap on a thread of its own and keeps all but one switched off, so an event pays the round trip and little more. The product owner rules it within the limit, 10 ms at the median by kind of event: no fault. As Arbor ships there is no tap (`Settings.pointerGestures` is false), and the taps' share is not paid at all.

entries.expected: What Arbor does itself is not reported back to it: the fake's `setFrame` emitted nothing. One move would at most be one report, with the final frame.
entries.happened: Every `setFrame` that changes something comes back as one to three `windowChanged` (resized where it stood, moved, resized again), each with the window's frame of that moment, after the controller's handler has returned. One that changes nothing has no echo, and all of a layout's calls are made before any echo is heard. None of it is the person's doing. Each echo was read with two calls on the main thread right after the command. In a later comparison with a rehearsal one `setFrame` had two to four echoes on the Mac, because a move and a resize are reported apart and some twice, where `FakeWindowSystem.deliverEchoes` sends one: 46 of its 319 differences. How many there are follows a rule, read off the recordings since: one for each step of the frame plan (size, place, size; or the place alone) that changes something, so one for a move or a resize alone and two for both; a third when the new size does not fit on the display at the old place, where macOS cuts the first resize short. It holds for some nineteen in twenty bundles of calls in the committed traces; the others bring one report more, after a drop. At the seam nearly all carry the final frame (213 of 215 in those traces), whatever the window's frame of that moment was: the layer reads the frame when a report arrives, which is after the call. They come 4 to 400 ms after the call.
entries.found: A recording of Accessibility notifications and traces of test windows and real apps on a hosted Mac (drag-to-edge, finder-commands, calculator-commands), and a performance review's measurements on a Mac.
entries.copes: EchoFilter.judge takes any report about a window within 0.15 s of Arbor's move for an echo, and a report of the frame it was given for a second. The fake queues as many echoes as the rule says, all with the final frame and all at the end of the command: not the odd fourth, nor how late they come. Not reading a fresh echo at all is named in the backlog and is not in the tree.

entries.happened: Nobody knows: what a hand on a real keyboard and a real mouse or trackpad gets, and what other apps' windows make of it. `input-taps.sh`, of which only a first version had run before (70 of 70), ran as it stands for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `8aa9e10`, macOS 26.6.2, once, started by hand, every key, click and scroll a posted event; its output is not in the repository). On the present keys everything was green on test windows and a witness at the far end of the taps: a ⌃⌥-click handed back once and in order (7 of 7), a ⌃⌥ double-click with its click counts (3 of 3), a ⌃⌥-drag of which nothing reaches the app, with the band and the framing (8 of 8), the ⇧-drag from the bare Desktop (6 of 6), posted pinches (7 of 7), and Arbor killed in the middle of a ⌃⌥-drag (3 of 3). entries.expected: F08: a display that is unplugged and plugged in again gets its arrangement back, and windows on other macOS Spaces are not lost from the tree.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: what a real cable, a lid, sleep or a change of Spaces does, and in which order macOS reports windows and displays. A second display can be made on a hosted Mac (`vdisplay.m`), and `check-displays.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `8aa9e10`, macOS 26.6.2, once, started by hand, every key, click and scroll a posted event; its output is not in the repository): 110 passed, 19 failed. What held: with the display on the right, on the left (negative x), above (negative y) and low on the right, Arbor's frame for it is macOS's, every docked window is in its slot and every overlay within a display; a frame on one display leaves the other alone, and windows out of view show on neither; unplugged, every window is on the screen that is left and belongs to it (13 of 13); plugged in again under the same identifier, what was docked there is docked there again; a Retina display in its place (9 of 9); quit with two displays and then unplug (6 of 6). What failed: 18 checks stand on long drags across displays that Arbor did not take for drags, or follow from one (a-dragged-window-may-stand-still-until-the-pointer-is-24-points-away; the board, 1.33, where they are still being read), and one on an expectation older than F61. `check-desktop.sh`, which has the Spaces, has not run. No recording in the repository holds a change of displays or of Spaces, and 246 tests rest on `setDisplays`. The spec still says "pending a machine with Accessibility permission".

entries.expected: F13: a download opens, `make install` gives Arbor an identity under which its permission survives the next build, an update is offered, and Arbor opens at login.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: what a person's own hands get: the dialog answered on their own login keychain, the switch flipped in System Settings, a release downloaded and put in the old one's place, a login after which Arbor is there. What scripts can ask has been asked, on hosted Macs on 2026-10-15 (plain branches of the hour, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, Reduce Motion on, each run once, every key and click a posted event; the outputs are not in the repository). `check-F13.sh`: first 11 passed and 2 failed, and an end in its second step of ten (the-imported-key-is-filed-under-another-label-than-the-tool-looks-for; codesign-finds-no-identity-in-a-keychain-that-is-on-no-search-list). Then, the tool written anew and the script cured, all ten steps: 80 passed and 4 failed, all four the script's own (doctor-fails-on-a-mac-as-it-comes; tmp-is-private-tmp): builds signed ad hoc and with the identity, installing, a different build with the same requirement, uninstalling, both windows about updates, the hardened runtime, `make release` for both architectures, `--remove`. `check-F13-system.sh`: first 20 passed and 6 failed, none of them Arbor's: macOS asked in a dialog for a keychain of the script's own under ~/Library/Keychains, nobody answered, the tool took certificate and key out again as it promises, and every build of that run was ad hoc. That run ended with exit code 0 and without its count: the script had unset a variable that `lib.sh`'s last lines read. Then, mended, 27 passed and 1 failed (tccutil-knows-a-bundle-only-from-where-and-by-whom-it-was-opened). A grant made to one build held for the next, which was different code under the same identity and ran without being granted anything: that is what `make install` promises. An ad-hoc build in between did not inherit it, macOS rewrote the entry to denied, and the signed build after it waited too (a-permission-belongs-to-a-signature). Arbor's entry among the login items is enabled when asked for, survives a new build copied over the old one, and is listed as disabled after `make uninstall`. A downloaded copy signed ad hoc is "Not Opened", with Move to Trash and Done; a process of it is listed meanwhile, which is no sign that it runs: only an answer on the control socket is. `check-signing.sh` in the same run, 56 of 56, walked the road the guide recommends, in a keychain of its own in the account's ~/Library/Keychains: the dialog, the password, Always Allow, and nobody is asked again. What stands between that and a person: the grant was a row written into the permission database, its daemon restarted and the notice posted that System Settings posts; the password was the script's own; nobody logged out and in; there is no published release, so none has been taken. `watchdog-bundle.sh` has never run. None of these scripts can be rehearsed (no keychain, no `codesign`); `release-tools-test.sh` runs against stand-ins for the macOS tools; nothing automatic starts any of them. Everybody installs.

entries.expected: F20: ⌃⌥N opens a field, a name is typed, ↩ gives it to the space in view, and the keyboard is back with the app that had it.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: whether a click elsewhere closes the field, and who has the keyboard then. `check-F20.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk of between 02:20 and 02:55 UTC, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository): 28 passed, 3 failed. Shown with real keys: the field gets what is typed, capital and all, without Arbor becoming the active app; no key reached the app while it was open; ↩, ⎋, ⌃⌥N again, a move of the view and a pause close it. Not shown by that script: every key pressed after a close was one of Arbor's own hot keys, which says nothing about who has the keyboard. That the keyboard goes back was shown later the same night by `check-keyboard-returns.sh` on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `0951b7f3`, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, Reduce Motion on, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository): with an app in front that writes down every key it is given, a plain x reached it before the panel came, did not while the panel had the keyboard, and did again afterwards; 128 of 128, once with an app Arbor arranges and once with one it does not look at. The app stayed the active one throughout. For the field: closed by ⎋, by ↩ and by ⌃⌥N (the board, 1.13). In `check-F20.sh` two greens compared nothing with nothing, because `pointer front` answers nothing on hosted Macs (the-rehearsal-never-runs-the-real-test-app). All three reds are the script's, mended since; its rehearsal now passes 32 of 32. Its click elsewhere landed on the field itself (a-press-on-the-name-field-stops-at-the-field), with one more red in its wake, and "the name is gone" failed because a click on the middle of the menu bar item had shown the Desktop (a-click-in-the-middle-of-the-menu-bar-item-presses-a-button). To the eye the reason for a refused name is cut off and carries backticks. Nothing automatic starts the script. The spec still says "the field has not run on a Mac".

Three real clicks in the map were taken by it and acted on. A click through a map that only passes by reached the app, but only the trace proves it: the script's checks there could not fail. The script's "click beside the map" lies in the panel's own padding and was taken by Arbor, so a click outside the panel was never tried. Place and size are fine on 1024×768. To the eye one thing is not: the-minimaps-windows-out-of-view-cannot-be-told-from-the-panel-in-the-dark-look. Blur and translucency cannot be judged on these Macs (hosted-macs-draw-every-material-as-one-flat-colour). By itself the map ships off (`minimapDuration` 0); the key is a default shortcut. Nothing automatic starts the script. The spec still says "nobody has seen the panel yet".

entries.happened: Nobody knows: who gets a key pressed within the 65 to 156 ms after a click into a listed app in which its ⌃⌥ keys are still Arbor's; whether the app gets the ⌃⌥-drag, a pinch or a scroll; the listed app's own windows docked; a real Emacs, remote desktop or virtual machine. `check-F41.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `0951b7f3`, macOS 26, one display of 1024×768, Reduce Motion on, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository): 51 passed, 2 failed, both the script's own: its app had lost the keyboard before the second `pass-through` (no-focused-window-that-arbor-knows-is-taken-for-nobody-at-the-keyboard). What held: in the listed app four shortcuts reached the app and not Arbor, one shortcut stayed registered and no tap was left; ⌃⌥⎋ answered there; after ⌘Tab away fifty-two shortcuts were back in 3 ms and the taps in 20; `pauseForApps` paused 8 ms after the app came forward and had resumed 52 ms after it left; both menus say so, in the pictures. Registering forty-five hot keys takes 1.3 ms at the median; in Arbor going to one shortcut took up to 23 ms of the main thread. A press passed on with `postToPid` arrived twice of twice, within a millisecond, and did not come back as a hot key. The round "a key pressed straight after the switch, ten times each way" was void: the app was off the list by then, and the keys came 215 to 457 ms after the switch, later than the gap. A trace ends at a pause, so none covers what came after the first.

entries.expected: F44: a shortcut is the key that bears its letter on the layout in use, the menu shows that letter, and a change of layout reaches Arbor in the background.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: what a real keyboard of another country does (ISO against ANSI; only one keyboard type was seen); whether Arbor hears of a switch to a layout without Latin letters; who gets ⌃⌥Space with two layouts enabled; a press within the first fifth of a second after a switch. `check-F44.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `0951b7f3`, macOS 26.6.2, keyboard type 198, once, every key a posted event; its output is not in the repository): 53 of 53, fifteen of them the harness's own. Told to go by German, French and Dvorak while US stayed selected, Arbor ran the right command for 22 keys pressed by position, each once, and nothing for the two that should run nothing; with `shortcutsFollowLayout` off the positions were a US keyboard's again. German and Dvorak were really selected while Arbor ran in the background: it had registered its 54 shortcuts anew 0.155 s and 0.028 s after the test app heard of the switch, and the next press went by the new layout. For those 0.155 s the old positions were still registered. The menu shows ⌃⌥Ü and ⌃⌥+ on German, in the picture. What proves nothing: Russian (no line in Arbor's log and no new registration, which is also what a deaf Arbor would show; the key pressed was one left over from Dvorak); the position shortcut on German, where k is where it is in the US; "how soon" printed Arbor's own two lines and no time of macOS's. The step about ⌃⌥Space skipped itself with a note. French, which criterion 5 names, was never really selected. A trace holds neither the layout nor its change, so none can replay F44.

entries.expected: F49: a pinned window keeps its place through every move of the view and stays in front, and the keyboard stays where it was. It is an item of the menu.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: whether a pin is in front again after a real click under it, and what Float All does to a pin that something other than a hand has moved. `check-F49.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk of between 02:20 and 02:55 UTC, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository), with its virtual second display: 95 passed, 19 failed. 17 of the reds are the known raise or follow from it (raise-does-not-lift-a-window-over-the-active-apps-key-window): the call lay wholly hidden behind the framed editor while `state` said pinned. So what the script asks about the front could not be seen, and will be asked anew once Keep in View makes room instead (the board, 1.25). The run brought out two faults of Arbor's own that arbor-sim plays just as well, so they are the board's and no cases here: a pin that a hand left with under half of it showing is pulled in at the next layout (251 points on the Mac), and a pin that comes back with its display loses its overhang (40 points). A third was only read from the code and one picture then, and is recorded since: at the mended script's second run (98 passed, 16 failed; the trunk at `9b4cd51e`) the call, which no hand had moved, is at 544,51 after Quit and after the relaunch, and not at 515,42 where it was (the board, 1.69); it had been through the main display's change of resolution (plugging-in-the-virtual-display-changes-the-main-one). Of that run's other reds eleven are the raise and two follow from it. The pin that is pulled in was not tried again: the mended script no longer leaves it hanging over. One fault was the script's, mended since: it dragged the call 251 points off the display and then pressed at x -11. Nothing automatic starts the script. The spec still says "is written and has not run".

A tap stays; a tap with ⌃⌥ kept down; hold, point, let go; a slow press; ⎋; the arrow keys; ⌃⌥ coming up before Space; auto-repeat; a click; another shortcut during the hold. So Carbon reports the release of a posted hot key with and without the modifiers. A suite of real-window checks that is not on the trunk yet had held and let go a peek the day before, green too. Whether a keyboard's own auto-repeat and a hand's order of letting go look like the posted ones is what is left, and nothing automatic starts the script. The spec still says "not yet compiled or run on a Mac". If a release is missed or misread the view springs back, and the window stays out of view.

entries.expected: F58: while the view is held nothing that is out of view comes into it, whatever comes forward, and when the hold ends or Arbor quits everything that waited is there again. It is an item of the menu.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: what a held view shows once the window in it is gone, since Arbor fetched it back (a-raise-fetches-a-minimized-window-out-of-the-dock); what an audience sees while displays change (macos-puts-windows-that-are-out-of-view-into-view-when-displays-change); where keys land that are typed in the 9 to 35 ms for which the keyboard is out of view; new windows, rules and dialogs during a hold; `hold <minutes>`; the sensors, which ship off. `check-F58.sh` ran for the first time on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk at `0951b7f3`, macOS 26, one display of 1024×768, Reduce Motion on, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository): 81 passed, 2 failed, both the script's own (it took a Dock that four thumbnails had made five points lower for a view that had moved). What held, borne out by the trace: six keys and ⌃⌥⇧F reached Arbor and were refused; a drag showed no preview and the drop went back in one move; an app that came forward by itself had the keyboard for 14 to 17 ms, by ⌘Tab for 9 to 12, a restored window for 32 to 34; no frame Arbor set put a window that was out of view into view; ⌃⌥⎋ released and moved nothing; holding still followed ⌘Tab; Quit took one move a window. Forty of the 81 are Arbor's own word for "out of view", not the window server's. "Kept down for three seconds" could not fail: a posted key does not repeat. The tool that asks ScreenCaptureKit for a picture of one window fell over twice and nothing went red. All three are mended in the script.

entries.expected: F63: when Accessibility is taken from a running Arbor, within three seconds the icon changes and a window asks for the permission back, mouse and keyboard keep working, and once it is given back every window is in view.
entries.happened: Nobody knows: whether the four ways home answer while the permission is gone, and what happens when a hand flips the switch in System Settings. What becomes of input meanwhile is known from probes that take the permission from Arbor alone (all-input-is-dropped-from-the-loss-of-the-permission-until-arbors-taps-are-gone). `check-F63.sh`, mended after its first run (a-process-started-without-the-permission-goes-on-hearing-no), got through on a hosted Mac on 2026-10-15 (the trunk of between 02:20 and 02:55 UTC, macOS 26.6.2, one display of 1024×768, once, every key and click a posted event; its output is not in the repository), with `pointerGestures` on, which ships off: 30 passed, 1 failed. Launched without the permission Arbor waits and holds no tap; granted, it starts by itself and may make taps at once. The loss with two windows out of view was noticed in 0.58 s: the taps gone, the four ways home registered, the warning sign in the menu bar, the window "Arbor needs its permission back" up, and commands fail with the sentence. Given back: every window in view, the taps and 52 shortcuts back, Back returns to the view, and a real ⌃⌥Space works. With nothing out of view no shortcut is held. The one red is the script's: it took that window for something left over. `input-taps.sh` had seen the four taps let go within a second of the loss earlier that day (the-trusted-flag-may-go-on-saying-yes). The three grants were noticed after 7.7, 8.1 and 9.3 s, where criterion 10 says three; at a third run (32 of 32), with two seconds left to the daemon, after 6.6, 5.8 and 7.8 s. That is not Arbor's: it asks macOS once a second while the permission is gone, and had started 61 ms after the first yes; the seconds lie between the script's announcement and macOS's own yes to that process. What is left: no key and no click was tried between a loss and a grant, because the script's own tools cannot press by then: so that the four ways home answer is not shown either. The spec still says "the switch itself has not been tried".

A docked window that cannot grow to its slot was centred on half points. A later run gives the rule for a position: x goes down and y goes up, as if rounded down in AppKit's coordinates, whose y runs the other way. 596.5 became 596 (2 of 2); 55.5 became 56, 117.5 118, 72.5 73, 52.5 53 (9 of 9). entries.expected: Growth stops at the visible frame's bottom less 1, as the first traces had it (a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock). The fake's `setFrame` took that point off the bottom of every visible frame, wherever the Dock is, until it was given the rule.
entries.happened: The point less belongs to the Dock. With the Dock at the bottom of the window's display growth stops at the visible bottom less 1: 17 answers of the 17 on the test window that were cut by more than 8 points, 40 of 40 on apps that take any height. So a slot that ends at the visible bottom is a point short in every order of the calls (8 of 8, on 1024×768 and on 1920×1080), and one that ends a point above is whole. With the Dock at the left or hidden the visible bottom is the display's, 768, and growth goes all the way to it: 18 cut answers of 18 end at 768, and the same slots are whole. The same on the display of two that has no Dock: 600 of 600; 1080 of 1080 once the Dock had gone to the display below, where growth then ends at 1630 of a visible 1631. The Dock at the left holds nothing back: a window sent to x 0, 20 and −100 went there, and under the Dock it grew wider and taller as asked. At the right it does hold: with-the-dock-at-the-right-a-growing-window-stops-a-point-short-of-it.

entries.happened: What stays above is the window's own title bar, and title bars are not one height. Terminal and TextEdit kept 32 points, Finder, Calculator and System Settings 52: a toolbar is part of it. The test windows kept 32 in the first recordings and 28 (1023,677; 480×348, not 480×352) in every run since, on the same macOS 26.6 and the same display: only the build differed. An earlier reading (29, 26 and 47) held every trace against a visible frame that ends at 705, while in the traces of real apps the Dock is lower and it ends at 708, 710 and 711. With 32 in `World.titleBarHeight` and `FakeWindowSystem.whereMacOSPuts`, every frame, request and answer that holds a floating window's height or a parked window's place was 4 points off: 142 of the 307 differences of the first comparison of one script on a hosted Mac and in a rehearsal. A display without a Dock has not been measured, nor a title bar with a tab bar under it; and with several displays, which of them stops a window is still a guess that Arbor and the fake share. Again in a later run: asked 1023,767, the test windows stopped at 1023,677, 20 times of 20: the visible bottom less 28.

By the name none was found ("SecItemCopyMatching: The specified item could not be found in the keychain"), and `scripts/make-signing-identity.sh` called that a wrong password, three times over, to whoever typed the right one. Then it went on to its trial signature, and macOS asked for the same password a fourth time, in a dialog about a key called “identity”: the dialog goes by the name of the file the key came in. That was a fault of the script's. What a person did next is not known: the identity was in the keychain by then and stayed there unless it was removed. To leave the name out would have been no cure: the command then changes every signing key in the keychain, the person's own among them.

entries.expected: A tap whose owner has lost the right to tap is switched off by macOS for good, or at least told at once.
entries.happened: A fact about macOS that every author of a tap should know: macOS drops all input behind any active tap whose owner lost the right, for as long as such events come more often than about once a second; a second each otherwise. Each event the tap has asked for is swallowed and takes with it whatever follows for about a second (0.41 to 1.25 s): macOS's own timeout for a tap. Then input flows until the next such event. Measured with a bare tool that has one active tap on mouse-downs and an identity of its own, passes everything on and never lets go. It lost its permission by `tccutil` at once, and 5.8 s after the row was deleted and the daemon killed in silence. In dense streams nothing arrived for as long as the tool lived, 785 of 785 events for 8 s and 2,400 of 2,400 for 24 s. That was first read as "for ever", and is corrected by sixteen valid rounds with presses 800 ms and more apart. Killed, its tap goes and the next stream arrives whole. **The callback is told, late and wrongly.** "Disabled by timeout" arrives in place of the next event that gets through, 1.25 and 3.5 s after the press that caused it. In a dense stream nothing gets through, so no word comes. `tapIsEnabled` never turns to no, the window server's list still shows the tap as enabled, and the next press is swallowed again. "Its callback is never told" is taken back. **What starts it and what does not** (thirteen valid rounds, two of each, `tccutil`'s road, fifty presses a second). One tap in but switched off: 0 of 1,200 and 0 of 1,196 lost in the eight seconds after the withdrawal, with a trial tap saying no 98 and 121 ms after the deed: a tap that is off never starts the drop. One off and one on for a kind that never comes: 0 lost, twice: a switched-on tap without traffic starts nothing. Switched on only 3.6 s after the withdrawal: macOS does not refuse it, `tapIsEnabled` says on, and the drop begins that instant (430 and 426 lost, to the end). No tap but a global `NSEvent` monitor: 0 of 1,200 lost, twice, and the monitor goes on being served after its owner lost the permission (600 of 600 presses). So it is the taps, not the monitor; a tap that is in and off is harmless; and whoever switches one on should ask first, with a trial tap. Arbor's removal of its taps is what gives the Mac back (all-input-is-dropped-from-the-loss-of-the-permission-until-arbors-taps-are-gone).

entries.expected: The left half of a visible frame (0,31 1024×674) is (0,31 512×674).
entries.happened: Where `macTiling()` says that it tiles, macOS put the window at (-1,31 512×674), at (-1,32 512×674) and at (-1,32 513×674), while its preview promised the half itself: (-15,16 542×704), the half grown by 15. It is not the left half's doing but the travel's. A window whose size changes on the way comes to rest a hair short of the tile, in whole points: a point further left if it came from the left, a point wider if it shrank, a point lower if its lower edge came from below the tile's. That one rule gives all fifteen sightings whose start is known, on displays 1024 and 1600 wide, on macOS 26.6 and on 15.7 with its margins ((7,34 500×665) for a tile of (8,33 500×665)), with Notes, Safari, TextEdit, Calendar and test windows, with Arbor running and without: a wide Safari window that came from the left rested at (799,31 801×791) in the right half of (800,31 800×791); windows that came from the right rested exactly, in the right half and on the whole screen. A window that is only moved arrives: one of a fixed size at (0,248), Notes that had the tile's size already at (0,31). One sighting is a point off the rule: Mail, which goes no narrower than 872, rested at (729,32 872×791), a point past the right half. Where a quarter ends, and a height that shrinks, have not been measured. All of it on displays of scale 1.

entries.expected: A window dragged by its title bar stays under the pointer: the grip (pointer minus corner) is constant. On the fake Mac a window follows the pointer exactly, so after a posted drag its title bar is where the pointer's path put it.
entries.happened: macOS holds the window back for a while whenever one of its edges meets another window's, the Dock's or the screen's, and it does not catch up afterwards. The pointer that took hold 12 points below the top was 12 and 60 points off in one run, 100 and 112 in another; with live reflow 100 102 and 99 81. A window dragged while Arbor was paused ended at -28,311 where the pointer's path gave -159,388. For a script the point worked out for the title bar can then be off screen. Later runs give numbers. A window trailed a posted pointer by 40 to 130 points on one axis where its edges met others', in lumps of about 42, and by up to twenty elsewhere. With no Arbor running it was 49 points behind after a drag of 130 and never caught up. A window as tall as its slot stopped when its bottom edge met the Dock (y stayed at 54 while the pointer went on to 103), so it was let go higher up than the pointer's path says. In a resize, an edge flush with a neighbour's gave 9 of the 40 points asked for. `World.drag` keeps the window under the pointer and lets it hang off the screen. **At the Dock's line it is a wall, as far as 19 points went:** a synthetic pointer, Arbor not running, could not carry a window 319 high from y 364 to 404: it stopped at y 385, its foot at 704 of a visible 705, while x went on following and the pointer went 19 points further down alone, 5 of 5. By its keeper's reading of the 60 Hz samples y is 385 in every sample from then on, through half a second of movement and a second at rest. On the way up there is no slack: at the pointer's first step up the window rose, so the hold had changed for good (31 points below the top in place of 12). A window 200 high passed no line on the same way. Whether a longer or faster pull takes a window past the line is not shown. **And against the top, with no Arbor running** (a day's control on a hosted Mac of 1600×900, visible 31 to 822; another session's samples, read by the ledger's keeper, not in the tree): Calendar 1600×791 at y 109, its foot at the display's foot, pressed in the title bar and taken 121 points up and 616 to the left: x followed point for point and y stayed 109 in every sample with the button down, with 78 points of room above it. Preview 708×424 at y 35: x followed, y stayed 35 in 29 samples, 4 points of room not taken. One run, two apps, both drags slanting; a straight pull, a slower hand and a window with much room were not tried.

No press tells them from an app's whim. Measured on macOS 26 with the real pointer on TextEdit and Terminal, in milliseconds after the release: ⌥-click on the green button, the first new frame after 59 to 110, in one step; Window ▸ Zoom after 399 to 408 (the menu blinks first), in one step; Fill in ten steps to 724; Move & Resize ▸ Left from 409 to 735, in ten to twelve steps no more than 75 apart. entries.expected: A window that moves without Arbor's doing was moved by its user. The controller hears that the displays changed, then of the moves macOS makes because of it. The stand-in's plain change of displays moves no window at all, which no Mac does.
entries.happened: When a display goes, macOS moves its windows onto the displays that remain at once. The Accessibility layer holds its report of the displays back until 1.5 s after the last of several notices, so the windows' own reports reach the controller first; it was feared that they are judged by the old displays. Taken for the person's own moves, they gave floating and pinned windows a new home, which did not go back with their display, and docked windows were sent to where no display was. After a display that only blinked there is no report at all, so nothing put the windows back. **Recorded since** (17 traces, one virtual display on a hosted Mac). A display comes: the active Space changes at 0.139 s, the screens' word at 0.178, all five windows' moves and resizes at 0.299 to 0.304, within 5 ms of one another, and Arbor's `displaysChanged` at 1.827. It goes: the word at 0.105, the windows one after another from 0.122 to 0.218, a second word at 0.215 in the midst of them, `displaysChanged` at 1.770. In all: the screens' word first; the windows 20 to 150 ms after it, within 5 to 100 ms of one another; all before the controller hears `displaysChanged`, 1.65 s after the word, which is Arbor's own wait; and every such report reaches the controller as a hand's. But macOS's own list of displays is already the new one at the first window's report, in all 17, so `Controller.knowsTheDisplays` sees that it does not know them and turns those reports away. That is none of the stand-ins' three guesses as they stand: their "windows first" reports while the stand-in's list is still the old one, which no recording has; what it finds beyond the recorded order (a shift made twice, a hop, a wrong display) is the lab's alone until a real cable, dock or lid says otherwise. Windows that never speak were not seen. What else macOS does then: macos-puts-windows-back-on-a-display-that-returns. **A second recording**, by a session that did not know of the first: macOS's raw notice at 55.286 s, fourteen reports of a changed window, each as a hand's, from 55.302 to 55.373, and the settled report of the displays at 57.199.

entries.expected: `RegisterEventHotKey` fails for a shortcut that another app already holds, so a refusal tells Arbor which keys are not its own: `HotKeyCenter.register` logs "shortcuts already in use by another app", and `doctor` names them. A hot key that is registered "swallows the key press so the frontmost app never sees it". This case said the first for as long as it stood, from the code's own words; no run was named.
entries.happened: On the one Mac that was asked `RegisterEventHotKey` never refused: it answered 0 to Arbor and to the other, in both orders, plain and exclusive. **Another process holds the chord, plain:** both hear every press; the app in front gets nothing. **Another process holds it with `kEventHotKeyExclusive`:** only that process hears, whoever came first. Arbor logs "registered 52 shortcuts" and `doctor` says "✔ Shortcuts: 52 registered": Arbor does not know that the key is not its own. **The app in front has a Carbon hot key of its own on the chord** (what Electron's `globalShortcut` is said to be): both ran, whoever registered first. **What a held key does keep from the app:** a menu item with the chord did not run, and a local and a global monitor in the app heard nothing. A listen-only event tap at the session level heard the key go down. So the road that Arbor is built for, the refusal, was never taken, and the two it has no eye for were: a key that is shared, and a key that is lost without a word. **On the first build's own binary too**, by a second probe: a rival with the same 52 hot keys, registered after Arbor and, in another session, before it, was refused none of 52, nor was Arbor; both heard every one of 51 keys, no app got any, and Arbor noticed nothing.
