entries.expected: What Arbor keeps out of view stays there while a display comes or goes; with the view held that is a promise to an audience.
entries.happened: When the virtual display came, macOS itself put all four windows that were out of view in plain view, at frames of before Arbor touched them (480×348 at 582,300, 450,372, 715,227 and 582,300), and the window shown at 0,424. The report of the displays reached the controller 1.85 s later, after the 1.5 s the app waits for displays to settle, and Arbor put all five right within twenty milliseconds. At the unplugging the same, for 1.75 s. The reports of those windows' moves came at once and were not acted on. Each window out of view was also given the same frame twice per change. **Both things that were not known then are known since**, from the mended script's run. It is not the change of the main display's size (plugging-in-the-virtual-display-changes-the-main-one): with two displays up a third came and went, the main one kept its 1920×1080, which the script checks, and macOS moved all five windows within 0.15 s, to the same places both times: the four to the middle of the main display, and the window shown to -524,539 at 1000×656, moved and made smaller, half on the third display, so that nothing covers the four. Arbor put all five back 1.6 to 1.7 s later at the coming and 1.5 to 1.6 s at the going. And it shows: in the first picture of each film three of the four stand in a cascade in the middle of the main display, titles and contents to read (the fourth has the frame of one of them and lies behind it). The script's own number, "the most of a window on a display", is geometry, the window server's frame against the displays, and does not know what covers what; that the windows could be seen rests on those two pictures and on the shown window's frame in the trace. Only the first picture of a film falls into the span, a picture taking about a second with three displays; the third display was never photographed. Ruled by the product owner: under a held view, while Arbor waits for the displays to settle, whenever macOS speaks of the screens or of one of those windows, what the hold keeps out of view is put away again at once; "a moment", not "never" (macoss-last-word-about-the-screens-comes-before-most-of-the-windows-reports).

Measured since: a running process learns of a grant or a loss only through the distributed notification `com.apple.accessibility.api`, and the flag follows that. entries.expected: What a stand-in plays of macOS's own doings does not depend on whether Arbor runs.
entries.happened: `FakeWindowSystem.open` gave a new window the keyboard, and `setMinimized` handed it on to the app's next window, only while Arbor was started. So every scene whose windows are opened before the start began with the keyboard nowhere, and copies of a world made for a relaunch lost who had it. On a Mac that is one state of several: the keyboard is on the Desktop after a click on the wallpaper, and otherwise in some window. In a walk played without Arbor as a control, an app's second window never came forward at ⌘M on its first, and with Arbor it did: one act in 5,378 was booked against Arbor that was the fake's. When both were made to happen regardless, 17 tests of 6,843 fell: ten scenes meant "nobody has had the keyboard", or one window in particular, and now say so; seven copied a world and now carry over who had it.

entries.expected: When the workspace says that an app became active (what the controller hears as `applicationActivated`), NSWorkspace's frontmostApplication names that app. The Accessibility layer leans on it: it drops the focus report of any app that is not named as the one in front.
entries.happened: The notice outruns the property. An app came forward while another was still named as the one in front 27 times in three runs (10, 8 and 9), and in five of the six activations of the one stretch that was traced. Arbor hears of the switch and throws it away, so the view does not move to the window the person switched to. The step goes red only in some runs. The lag belongs to activations that a program asks for: 5 to 107 ms. Through Launch Services 0 of 12 lagged, of posted clicks 1 in about 24 (17 ms), of ⌘Tab 0 of 6. A click on another window of the other app is lost as well, not only ⌘Tab: `AXFocusedWindowChanged` and `AXMainWindowChanged` come about 2 ms after the press, before the notice, when even a prompt NSWorkspace still names the old app, so both are dropped; with a fresh property the notice makes up for it, with a stale one nothing does. What the cure does not reach: a-pause-for-an-app-ends-inside-the-notice-and-reads-the-old-focus.
entries.found: A probe build with extra log lines: the real-window run played three times on one hosted Mac, with the step repeated and a trace running. Later the real layer run on Linux against a model of a Mac, held to lags of 5 and of 50 ms: it reports that the keyboard moved, twice, and never a focus. That the two Accessibility reports of a click come before the notice is a guess from the traces' delays.

In full screen the window cannot be asked (the position is refused, the size accepted and forgotten), so nobody outside the app can change that. The picture arrives at the old frame and, as it ends, the window stands in its slot: a cut.

entries.expected: While a window is dragged its app reports every move: one "moved" for each mouse event, with the window exactly under the pointer. So the last reported frame is where the window was let go. The fakes send an exact change before every `dragMoved`.
entries.happened: The window server moves a dragged window itself and knows its place at once. The app hears about a tenth of a second later and posts eight to ten notices a second, and some apps post none until the drag is over. So the reported frame lags the pointer, also at the release: after a quick drag released at once the last frame reported was 170 points behind. The preview lagged, and a window dropped on the Desktop was remembered short of where it was let go. A read from the window server costs about as much as one from the app (0.18 ms) and cannot hang on the app. Into how many runs of moves one drag is reported differs from one playing to the next, with how often the preview changes on the way.

entries.expected: A change marked as somebody's own doing means that somebody moved or resized the window. The stand-in reports a new title, and an app hidden or shown, as such a change (`userInitiated: true`).
entries.happened: Terminals and browsers change titles all the time, and Terminal renames itself with every resize, before the resize is reported. When the traces were recorded the real layer read the whole window at a new title and reported it as somebody's doing: with the same frame, or for Terminal with the new frame, ahead of the echo of Arbor's own call. Today the real layer reads the title alone and reports it with `userInitiated: false`, as it does for an app hidden or shown. `FakeWindowSystem.setTitle` and `setHidden` went on saying true, so the fake disagreed with the real layer, as the older traces still do: they stay as they were recorded. The first comparison of a hosted Mac with a rehearsal showed it at once: every window of an app that hides or shows again is nobody's doing on the Mac and the person's in the rehearsal. When the stand-in was made to say what the real layer says, one test of 5,810 fell, which pinned the words; no fault of Arbor's showed.
entries.found: The traces title-change, terminal-commands and terminal-edge from a hosted Mac, then reading the real layer and the stand-in side by side.

entries.expected: The first posted press and drag of the real-pointer test moves the window.
entries.happened: In the first whole run on a hosted Mac the first drag moved nothing: no preview, no dock, the window still at (270, 140), and all that built on it failed (7 passed, 11 failed). The step began about nineteen minutes into a job on a Mac nobody had touched. In a job of its own, four minutes after the start, the same script has passed 18 of 18 five times. A screen saver was suspected and tried: with one up the first drag went through. It happened again thirteen minutes into a loaded job, again 7 and 11: pointer events arrive, windows move, macOS tiles, and Arbor sees no drag and logs nothing. Two mechanisms of Arbor's were suspected here, and that is taken back: late in such a job a system alert (UserNotificationCenter's, 260 by 250 at 382,118, at the modal level) lay over the title bars where the script presses. The drags that went unseen late in a job were not Arbor's.

entries.expected: `AXIsProcessTrusted()` says whether Arbor may use Accessibility.
entries.happened: The flag can go on saying yes after Arbor is removed from the list with the − button, and one no out of the blue may only be the privacy daemon restarting. Seen since, on macOS 26.6.2: under a second after `sudo tccutil reset Accessibility` a running Arbor logged "Accessibility permission is gone (AXIsProcessTrusted says yes, but macOS refused a tap)". The thorough question caught it, and the four taps were gone within one second. The stand-in's comment still calls `flagLags` unseen. Measured since: behind the daemon's back (the row deleted, the daemon restarted, nothing announced) the loss reached a running process after 3.95, 4.7, 6.9, 9.97, 13.8, 14.3, 15.97 and more than 30 s, and it showed by a refused tap while the flag still said yes. With `tccutil reset` the withdrawal is immediate. The longest yet on the silent road: 21.65 s. And after `tccutil reset` a bare tapper's flag never turned at all, in 12 s: only a trial tap said no (all-input-is-dropped-from-the-loss-of-the-permission-until-arbors-taps-are-gone).

entries.expected: Once the Accessibility call has returned, or arborctl has answered, the window server's list shows the window at its new place.
entries.happened: The window server applies moves a moment later, so a check that looks at once fails. The first real-window run passed 40 of 42: both failures were the runner reading windows sent out of view too early. Rectangles are compared to within three points since. Measured since, without Arbor, on eleven apps and the test window: read right after Accessibility's answer the list differed from it in 143 results of 170. Of 615 calls that changed a frame it still had the frame from before the call after 475, something older after 94, the new one after 46. At the first later look, 62 to 209 ms after the call, it had caught up in 165 of 170; at the second, 200 ms and later, in all. `FakeWindowSystem.stackedWindows` was never behind. Made to be, for 0.15 s, one test of 7,398 fell, and it showed a fault: of two commands within that time the second finds the windows that the first fetched still listed in their corner, takes that for macOS showing its desktop (`SweptAside.isSwept`) and raises no stage, so with motion on it jumps. The Accessibility layer asks the same question at a press. **It can show a stage of the road:** the five that were behind at the first look, all on the test window after calls back to back, listed a half-way frame 62 to 146 ms after the last call (back from the corner by size, position, size: 1023,677 494×650, the new size at the old place). The same with Arbor running: after `float-all` one call of Arbor's, from 518,43 494×650 to 220,180 480×348, was answered whole in 2.2 ms, AXResized and AXMoved came within 6 ms, and the list, read by a script of the real-window suite a moment later, gave 518 43 480 348: the plan's first stage, a frame nobody asked for. In a hand it is the same: right after a size call with the button down the list was still old in 53 of 58, and new at 50 ms in 63 of 64. Accessibility's own answer did not move afterwards (a-stale-read-back-makes-arbors-own-move-the-persons).

entries.expected: A path is spelt one way.
entries.happened: macOS's /tmp is a link to /private/tmp, and that is how `ps` spells the path of a program that runs from there: what was started from /tmp/arbor-x is listed under /private/tmp/arbor-x. On Linux, where the harness's own tests run, /tmp is /tmp. And the other way about: of a copy that runs from /private/tmp/… the app is listed there, and its watchdog, which Arbor starts by its bundle's own idea of the path (`Bundle.main.executableURL`), under /tmp/…: "21076 /private/tmp/…/Arbor" and "21081 /tmp/…/Arbor --watchdog 21076", side by side. A search that begins at either spelling finds one of the two. So four checks that "nothing is left running" could not have seen a watchdog, and `make install`, had it had to stop such a copy by force, would have killed the app with its watchdog looking on, which starts it again.

Each of the cures that met there passes alone. Proven line by line on the model, and the reading confirmed by the author of the sweep's cure: the press at 300,112 is served 0.3 s late, when the window server has the window at 157,143. The first look finds no window and leaves the press open; a second look, at the pointer's place of now, finds it 71 points from where Accessibility last had it, over the lead of 32 for which `WindowGrab.isListedElsewhere` takes a window to be swept aside and in nobody's hand: settled. entries.expected: While a window is held at an edge, Arbor's drop preview (`showDropPreview`) is the only one on the screen.
entries.happened: Where macOS tiles it shows a preview of its own at the same time: two windows owned by WindowManager at level 0, the tile grown by 15 points on every side (-15,16 542×704 for the left half of a 1024×768 display, -15,16 1054×704 for the whole). Arbor's blue outline (12,43 494×650) lies inside macOS's white one and promises something else. It was first seen at the edge between two displays; the earlier drags to an outer edge had stopped three points short of it. At the top edge it has also been seen the other way round: in a day with real apps macOS's preview never came up while Arbor's was up, though without Arbor it does. What is left since Arbor stands aside (the board, 1.30): on its way to an edge that is macOS's the pointer crosses Arbor's band, so Arbor's preview is up from 11 points to 1 and gone at 0, one preview after the other. Counted since in the sampler's logs: 63 appearances, always two windows with one frame, the tile grown by 15, one right in front of the dragged window and one right behind it (three times with a sheet between); 60 went within 64 ms of the release. NOT PLAYED by the fake Mac: the top edge seen the other way round; the edge between two displays (it has one display); the 113 ms in which both previews were up on the way to an edge; a tile that is what another tiled window leaves over; a preview that goes again with the button down.

The stand-ins know where macOS acts, and the fake Mac lists macOS's preview round the held window.

entries.expected: Each script sent to a hosted Mac is a run of its own, of the commit it was sent from, and the Macs are served in the order of asking.
entries.happened: `run.sh` cuts a script's name to 16 characters for its tag, so two scripts that begin alike share one tag and the second dispatch cancels the first, unless `MAC_SHELL_TAG` tells them apart. A queued job checks out the branch's head when it starts, not the commit at the dispatch. GitHub does not serve queued Mac jobs in order, and for half an hour it lent about three Macs of five: runs waited 30 to 35 minutes. `run.sh` refuses a bare commit as what to run. And a cancelled run that somebody starts again is not seen by the `run.sh` that started it; its output can still be fetched over Git from its output branch.

Whether a person's two quick shortcuts do the same has not been tried. Seen again in a probe that pressed ⌃ over and over ("To start dictating, press the Control key twice"): the alert stood on the screen for some nine minutes, to the end of the run. There it took no key that could be found: the rounds after it are complete.

If the focus report beats the notice that the Space changed, that rescan does not know of a switch and reports one window replaced by the other (`windowReplaced`). The controller hands the first window's slot and all it knows about it to the second and forgets the first; on the way back the same in reverse. Whatever differed between the two Spaces' arrangements is gone. With the notice first all is well.

entries.expected: Out of view is out of sight.
entries.happened: Windows out of view show in Mission Control as miniatures like any other window. Looked at closely on 2026-10-15, with one window framed and four out of view at the display's corner: Mission Control and the app's own windows (⌃↓) show all five whole, title bar and content, the four at about half their own size (143×166 for 275×320, 143×340 for 275×653; the framed one 520×340 for 1000×653), and the Dock tells Accessibility of each as a button with the window's title. A click on the picture of a window that is out of view frames it in one move: the focus report, then two frames set within 8 ms, the picked window in and the old one out, and the picked window has the keyboard. So the way a Mac user already knows finds every window that Arbor has put aside. **With the view held the pick is turned away in silence:** macOS gave the picked window the keyboard twice, 0.25 s apart, Arbor sent it back both times, and no line on screen says why (none in the log of that session, none in the two pictures of eight that were opened; the board, 1.71). Not tried: with motion (Reduce Motion was on, so Mission Control faded, where a person sees windows fly out of the corner and back), real apps, several displays or Spaces, the Dock's menu, ⌘`. What share pickers list, and whether four such windows leave a smudge of shadows in the corner, is not known.

entries.expected: A hot key that is registered for ⌃⌥A is Arbor's, whatever else is down. `docs/KEYBOARD.md`: "A global shortcut is taken away from every app on the Mac". `HotKeyCenter`: it "swallows the key press so the frontmost app never sees it".
entries.happened: With the flag that a held fn (Globe) key sets, 0x800000, on the key event, Arbor's keys that are not arrows are not Arbor's. Arbor running, 52 shortcuts registered, not paused, nothing on any list: ⌃⌥A, ⌃⌥↩, ⌃⌥Space, ⌃⌥[, ⌃⌥Z, ⌃⌥F and ⌃⌥G, seven of seven, reached the app in front (the tap at the annotated session point, the local monitor, `performKeyEquivalent`, then `keyDown` in the view), and Arbor's log did not grow by a line. ⌃⌥← and ⌃⌥→ with the flag went to Arbor as ever: an arrow carries it by nature, and posted without it an arrow reaches the app and not Arbor (posted-arrow-keys-need-the-flags-a-keyboard-adds, mirrored). So the window server compares that flag exactly when it looks for a hot key. With the flag AppKit's menu did not fire for the letters and the bracket, with Arbor or without; for ↩ and Space it did. So it fits an app that listens in its page or its view, not one with a plain menu equivalent for a letter. **What does not matter**, each 7 of 7 to Arbor and none to the app: the right-hand ⌃ and ⌥, left and right mixed, both of each pair down, Caps Lock's flag, the numeric-pad flag, flags with no modifier key going down at all, a key held to repeat. **Not shown:** that a real fn key held on a real keyboard puts that flag on a letter's key event as it passes the window server. On a laptop fn sits beside ⌃; if it does, a finger that catches fn with ⌃ turns ⌃⌥A into the app's own ⌃⌥A, with Arbor running and knowing nothing. One of two candidates for what a person met (a-key-arbor-does-not-hold-at-the-moment-reaches-the-app-in-front); it fits their words better in one respect, "Arbor running, not paused". The cure that was tried next, a second registration with Carbon's bit for fn, is heard (a-key-registered-with-fn-and-without-is-two-keys-or-one). No detector of the gate has an eye for a key of Arbor's that arrives elsewhere.
entries.found: A second probe, `probe-whose-key.sh`, one run on a hosted Mac (macOS 26.6.2) on the first build itself, its commit and the probe and nothing else: an app in front and a listener in the background with ears of every kind, taps at three points, monitors, a menu, a view, and Arbor's own log counted line by line: nine keys by thirteen hands and roads, beside the same thirteen with no Arbor. Every key was a posted event: no finger, no real keyboard.
entries.copes: HotKeyTable registers each shortcut that has one (`KeyChord.hasFnTwin`: ⌃ and ⌥ in it, a printing key, Space, ↩ or ⎋) a second time with fn, under one shortcut; the two come and go together. Seen on a hosted Mac (macOS 26.6.2, posted events, once; `mac-shell-out/whosekey.sum`): with fn's flag none of nine keys reached the app in front, where seven had on the first build, and each key's command ran once, as without the flag. On Apple's keyboards fn with an arrow, ↩ or ⌫ is another key altogether: there this does not help.

entries.expected: With ⌥ held during a drag macOS takes the window wherever the pointer is: it lands where the preview showed.
entries.happened: It has been seen both ways. A probe that held a window at one point after another and looked for macOS's preview among the window server's windows found it wherever the pointer was with ⌥ held, whatever else was held (⇧, ⌘, ⌃⌘, ⌃⇧): `MacTiling` is written from that, and says that macOS takes the window. That probe looked for the preview, not for where the window ended. In later probes that let go, with posted keys, ⌥ alone made macOS show its preview (the left half at x 200, the right half at x 512) and leave the window where it was let go, three times out of three, and no report followed the release. Ten more are in outputs that are kept, ten out of ten, five on macOS 26.6.2 and five on 15.7.9: all of one drag, the same test window to (200,368), the left half promised, ⌥ down before the press and up after the release, Arbor paused. ⌥ pressed in the middle of a drag has not been measured. By the name of its switch, "Hold ⌥ key while dragging windows to tile", macOS tiles. With ⌥⇧, ⌥⌘, ⌃⌥⌘ and ⌃⌥⇧ the same drag ended in the tile.

afterword: ## What the first person at a desk met

The maintainer worked with the first build for a session (build 179, commit `3deb36a`), then quit it and went back to macOS's own tiling. What they said is `collab/IDEAS.md`, I16 to I25, and `collab/HANDOFF-2026-10-14-maintainer.md` beside it; it is ruled on in `collab/QUESTIONS.md`, Q29, and heads `collab/BOARD.md` as section 0.
**Seven of ten were no fault by our own books, and the eighth hangs on a cause nobody can now read: the gap is not between the fake and the Mac but between the spec and the person.**

**What is counted.** The ten are the ten scenarios of `collab/scenarios/wanted`, one for each thing disliked. Nine are the maintainer's own; the tenth, the key that fills the screen, nobody has met yet: the product owner foresaw it from the third task of I24. I21 has no scenario and stands under the table. *A fault by our own books* means: at that commit a spec, a ruling, the keyboard map or the guide said that Arbor should do otherwise than it did. Each row is sorted by what the maintainer wrote, not by what its scenario asks besides.
- **Seven: no fault.** Arbor did what was written, and tests held it to that (of I18 nothing was written): I17, I18, I20 a, I20 b, I20 d with I20 e and I23, I22, the key that fills the screen.

- **Two: faults, known, ruled on and not built.** I19 (Q22, board 1.22) and I20 c (Q20, board 1.18). Our own instruments had found both, the product owner had ruled against both on 2026-10-14, and both were on the board when the build was cut. The tests still held Arbor to the old way.

- **One: open between two candidates, both being cured.** I16. If the first was theirs it is the eighth. If the second, it is a fault, and the first of the ten in which Arbor itself met a Mac that differs from what its books believe. In the product owner's words: seven, or eight if the likelier cause was theirs.

- **In nine of the ten the stand-ins and a Mac agree**, and where they differ is all that the rest of this page counts. The tenth is I16: no app in a stand-in has a shortcut of its own, so a key that Arbor gives back does nothing there, and no stand-in compares flags at all. At the head of the chain that may lie before the first candidate stands a script that expected of macOS what macOS 15 and 26 do not do, and whose check had never got past its second step on a Mac.
Names and numbers are as they stood at `3deb36a`, by grep. Whoever answers a complaint changes these tests; the table stays as the record of what held before.
| | What the person met | A fault by our own books? | What held Arbor to it, or said the contrary of what the person met | What would have caught it | Board |

| **I16** | On a tester's Mac, ⌃⌥A (`arrange`) with a widely used desktop chat app in front archived the open conversation in that app, twice in a row: the app's own ⌃⌥A ran | **Open between two candidates. Nobody has read the person's log, and nobody will ask.** **One, by the book:** another ad-hoc build over a grant made for the old one. Arbor waits for the permission and holds no key. Seen twice on hosted Macs, with posted keys: on the trunk's Arbor, and on the first build's own binary, where 52 of 52 keys reached an app. `status` says "waiting for Accessibility permission", `bindings` "all off without Accessibility permission", the item is a warning triangle, and the row in the database still says allowed. To hold no key then is by the book. `docs/features/F63-permission-taken-away.md`: Arbor "gives the shortcuts back to the apps"; criterion 5: "with none, no shortcut". `docs/GUIDE.md` knows the state ("this happens after installing a new build") and files it under "The shortcuts do nothing". *The chain that may lie before it, five links, each with its mark.* (1) *Proven on hosted Macs, macOS 15.7.9 and 26.6.2, not 14.8.9:* `security import` names every key it imports alike, so `scripts/make-signing-identity.sh`, which looks for its key by name, found none and called every failure a wrong password: whoever typed the right one was told three times that it was wrong. (2) *Follows for whoever is then without the identity; by reading the script, not from (1) alone:* `make install` signs ad hoc, the third choice of `scripts/sign.sh`, and says so in the middle of a build log. (3) *Known* ([a-permission-belongs-to-a-signature](#a-permission-belongs-to-a-signature)): to macOS that is a new app, and the old build's entry still looks switched on. (4), (5) *Seen on hosted Macs in that state, with posted keys:* Arbor waits and holds no key; ⌃⌥A reaches the app in front. *Not shown for that session.* Links 2 to 5 are by the book. The first is not: the script's own head says that the password typed there "saves the dialog". It is a difference of this page's own kind, and a case is on its way. **Two, not by the book:** with the flag of a held fn key on the key event, Arbor's letter keys are not Arbor's. Arbor running, 52 shortcuts registered, not paused, nothing on any list: ⌃⌥A, ⌃⌥↩, ⌃⌥Space, ⌃⌥[, ⌃⌥Z, ⌃⌥F and ⌃⌥G, seven of seven, reached the app in front, and Arbor's log did not grow by a line. On a laptop fn sits beside ⌃. *Not shown:* that a real fn key held on a real keyboard puts that flag on a letter's key event. `docs/KEYBOARD.md`: "A global shortcut is taken away from every app on the Mac". That would be the first of the ten in which Arbor itself met a Mac that differs from what we believed, which is this page's own matter. It fits the maintainer's own words better in one respect: "Arbor running, not paused". That ⌃⌥A was bound at all is by the book: the row "⌃⌥A, `arrange`, shipped" of the keyboard map, whose table of clashes names editors, IDEs, design tools and remote desktops, no chat app. The cases: [a-key-arbor-does-not-hold-at-the-moment-reaches-the-app-in-front](#a-key-arbor-does-not-hold-at-the-moment-reaches-the-app-in-front), [with-fns-flag-on-the-event-arbors-letter-keys-are-not-arbors](#with-fns-flag-on-the-event-arbors-letter-keys-are-not-arbors), [macos-never-refused-a-shortcut-that-another-process-holds](#macos-never-refused-a-shortcut-that-another-process-holds) | `withNothingOutOfViewNoShortcutIsHeld`: without the permission Arbor holds nothing. `defaultLabelsAreTheOnesTheMenuAlwaysShowed`: Arrange is ⌃⌥A. On the fake Mac "A registered hot key never reaches an app" (`World.pressKey`). No stand-in compares flags: a key there is the name of a chord. - **A ruling does not turn a test round.** After Q20 and Q22 the tests, a scenario and a check on CI's Macs went on asking for what had been overruled, so green meant that the fault was there. What follows, decided by the product owner on 2026-10-15: a ruling against the trunk comes the same day with its red scenario in `collab/scenarios/wanted`, with the list of the tests, scenarios and Mac checks that hold Arbor to what was overruled, and with a mark on each, so that their green is not counted as proof.

## The first regression that a Mac caught after it had landed

In the night of 2026-10-15 a change landed that was green in every test and rehearsal on Linux, and from then on the first dock on a Mac left the window short of its slot ([a-size-clipped-by-the-screen-was-taken-for-the-apps-refusal](#a-size-clipped-by-the-screen-was-taken-for-the-apps-refusal)). It was caught 43 minutes later by playing five journeys on a hosted Mac and in a rehearsal and comparing them line by line. Linux could not see it because the stand-ins let a window grow off the screen ([a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock](#a-window-asked-to-grow-stops-at-the-dock)); that they do not play what a size depends on had stood on this page, among the cases of ring 2, and nobody held the change against it. The five journeys cost about six and a half minutes of one hosted Mac, and from now on they are played at the trunk's head after every batch. **Its limits:** five journeys of test windows on one small display. No real apps, no second display, no app that hangs, no permission that goes. It caught this because a plain first dock meets it. **The cure has been seen on a Mac since**, by the same five journeys beside a control of the same night: 23 answers cut at the Dock's line and 0; 30 of 82 looks at a docked window short of its slot and 0 of 82; again on the trunk itself, with the Dock at either side and with two displays. What macOS does was then asked of it call by call, with Arbor not running, and with a hand on the window: `collab/reports/2026-10-15-how-far-a-window-grows.md`. The journeys with two displays found the next one: [a-size-call-right-after-a-change-of-display-is-judged-by-the-old-display](#a-size-call-right-after-a-change-of-display-is-judged-by-the-old-display).
## What the stand-ins say they cannot imitate
In their own words, with the place where they say it. Nothing in this list is a reproach: a stand-in that names its limits is worth more than one that does not.
**The fake Mac (`Sources/arbor-fakemac`, `scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`).** Files without a folder are in `Sources/arbor-fakemac`.
Whole subjects:

- It can say nothing about AppKit's and Accessibility's timing and order of notifications, animations, the finer points of which window is in front, the Dock growing and shrinking, Spaces and full screen, what anything looks like, or whether an event tap or a hot key really gets its events. "A rehearsal proves the script, not Arbor." (`main.swift`, `scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`, `docs/TESTING.md`)
- Every picture of a rehearsal is one black pixel. (`scripts/mac-shell/rehearse/mac-tools`, `scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`)

- It has one display. The tool that plugs in a virtual display has no stand-in, nor has the curtain. A script that plugs in a display, or compiles a tool of its own against AppKit, stops with exit code 2. (`main.swift`, `scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`, `docs/TESTING.md`, `scripts/mac-shell/check-F49.sh`)
- It has no full screen: "nothing here could say anything true". (`World+TestApps.swift`)
- It has neither dark mode nor macOS's Spaces. (`collab/BACKLOG.md`, K1851)

- It has no app but the test windows: no TextEdit, Terminal or Calculator to open, and `open` launches nothing. (`scripts/mac-shell/check-F54.sh`, `scripts/mac-shell/check-F53.sh`, `World+Arbor.swift`)
- "There is nothing in this world that Arbor cannot see." (`Arbor.swift`)
Time:
- A whole second passes after every line that changes something, so debounced work (saving, putting windows back) has always happened by the next line. (`main.swift`, `World.swift`)
- A `sleep` of under a second does nothing; a longer one moves the fake clock and takes no time. (`scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`, `World.swift`)

- How long the button is down, and how long a drag takes, are not modelled. An app that insists on its frame has done so, quick or slow, "by the time a quarter of a second is over". (`World+Pointer.swift`, `World+Pointer.swift`, `World+TestApps.swift`)
- Motion is recorded and not shown: the stage would be down again before anyone could look. (`Arbor.swift`)
- The date is a fixed day. (`World+Arbor.swift`)
- SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the stand-in for Arbor cannot say that it died; whoever comes next notices. (`Driver.swift`)
Copies that have to follow by hand:

- The decisions and log lines of the macOS-only code that scripts can see are repeated, each next to the name of what it repeats. When one of those changes, the fake Mac has to follow, and nothing says so. (`main.swift`, `World+Arbor.swift`, `collab/BACKLOG.md`, K219)

- Of the system's facts it has "the little … that this Mac has an answer to". A rescue runs "with permission and without the alert". Where the app beeps at a refused URL, nothing happens. (`Arbor.swift`, `World+Arbor.swift`, `World+Arbor.swift`)
- No Mac's compiler has seen it: it is declared on Linux only. (`Package.swift`)
Windows and who is in front:
- The order of windows is the world's own: "the fake knows nothing of clicks and of apps coming forward". (`Arbor.swift`)
- The heads-up line and the panel of shortcuts are "recorded and not listed among the windows yet". (`Arbor.swift`)
- The wallpaper and the icons on it are left out of the list that decides what is under the pointer. (`World+Input.swift`)

- The furniture (menu bar, Dock, Finder's Desktop, Control Center's items) is what one hosted Mac listed before any session, stretched to the display; Arbor's menu bar item is where that Mac's menu bar put it. (`World+Pointer.swift`, `World+Menu.swift`)

- Sheets hang on windows only; only ordinary windows in front can be minimized, restored or given a tab; a tab that is not in front can be neither closed nor given the keyboard. (`World+TestApps.swift`)

- Guessed, not measured: that a window shrunk with `setContentSize` keeps its top left corner; how far swept windows move up or down; a panel's title bar of 22 points. (`World+TestApps.swift`, `World+Pointer.swift`, `collab/BACKLOG.md`, M678)
Input and the menu:

- The right button is modelled on Arbor's menu bar item only. Only Arbor's own shortcuts can be held down. An open menu takes every key, and "only Escape is modelled". (`World+Input.swift`, `World+Input.swift`, `World+Input.swift`)
- The keyboard layout is the US one, and hot keys are registered "in a world where no other app holds a shortcut". (`World+Arbor.swift`, `World+Arbor.swift`)
- In Go to… the real palette chooses when the button comes up; "nothing here tells the two apart". (`World+GoTo.swift`)
- The menu's sizes are made up; it has one level of submenus; About Arbor opens no panel and Open Settings File no editor. (`World+Menu.swift`)
The Mac's own commands:

- Only some of what a script uses is a stand-in. `rm`, `pkill`, `osascript`, `tccutil` and the rest would be the real ones, which is why a rehearsal refuses to run on a Mac. (`scripts/mac-shell/rehearse.sh`)

- Each stand-in knows the few uses that the scripts make of it and refuses the rest, with a message that names it and exit code 64. `lsappinfo` knows two forms. (`scripts/mac-shell/rehearse/mac-tools`, `main.swift`, `World.swift`)
- Its pointer tool and its test app are stricter than the real ones on purpose: they refuse what they do not know, where the real ones stay silent. (`World+Pointer.swift`, `World+TestApps.swift`)
Said nowhere, but so, by the code:
- Accessibility is always granted, and the tool's questions about permissions always answer yes. (`World+Arbor.swift`, `World+Pointer.swift`)
- A hand edit of settings.json is noted for later replays and never applied: there is no stand-in for the app's `SettingsWatcher`. (`World.swift`, `Sources/ArborKit/App/SettingsWatcher.swift`)
- The peek's outline and the backdrop are not among Arbor's windows. (`collab/BACKLOG.md`, K1030)
- `killall` does nothing, so "restart WindowManager to make it read the setting" cannot be got wrong. (`scripts/mac-shell/rehearse/mac-tools`)

- Every window is a test window, with a title bar of 28 points as CI builds them, and a double-click on it and the green button both fill the screen or go back; the person's setting for the double-click is not asked. (`World.swift`, `World+Input.swift`)

Read as a whole:
- Five switches in `Echoes` are rude by default, all from one recording on macOS 26; since then macOS's tiling as well.

- Everything that imitates lateness (`focusIsSlow`, `defersFocus`, `restoresLate`, the two flights, `holdsEchoes`) is off by default and is switched on by 25 of 5560 tests. None of it is in arbor-sim, in the scenarios or in the fake Mac, and only `holdsEchoes` is in the chaos lab.

- No knob makes time pass while Arbor waits for an app, applies a call that timed out late, loses a destroy or a termination notice, moves other windows when one leaves full screen or an app is unhidden, nudges the Dock at a minimize, sends a focus report before "created", repeats a focus report, sends the half-way frame of a `setFrame`, lets a dragged window trail the pointer, stops a window at the menu bar, stops a raise short of the active app's key window, brings Finder forward when an app hides, delivers echoes app by app, or asks `WindowGrab` whether a drag is one.

- The chaos lab is polite too. Apps that fight back or hang appear only in the 30 % of runs that allow misbehaviour (`Sources/ArborTesting/ChaosGenerator.swift`). It never takes the permission away and never sets a size step, `stackingIsUnknown`, `flagLags` or `refusesTaps`. A failing script it does not know is only printed unless `ARBOR_CHAOS_STRICT=1`. Three of its rules are red by name today (`Sources/ArborTesting/ChaosKnownFailures.swift`).

- A new member of a seam that has a default implementation falls on that default behind the trace recorder, the replayer and the fake Mac until somebody forwards it, and nothing fails to compile. `TraceForwardingTests` is the net.

- **Once a stand-in has said the same as a Mac without being told.** Drags had been seen to go unnoticed on hosted Macs, and a run of the real-window suite had shown one with the pointer 27 points away at the first look. A model of a Mac under the real Accessibility layer (`make mac-on-linux`), asked only how a drag can be lost, came to the same lines of the layer by its own road, on Linux, and said more: a drag of any length is lost for good once the pointer is far away at the first look (a-dragged-window-may-stand-still-until-the-pointer-is-24-points-away). The first run of `check-displays.sh`, made in the same hour by somebody who did not know of either, lost three of four long drags. Every other case on this page is a stand-in corrected by a Mac; here one agreed with a Mac beforehand. What share the script's coarse steps had in that run is for its trace to say.

- **The model of a Mac guards by hand.** `scripts/mac-on-linux/build.sh` tells its stories about the real Accessibility layer and walks a rude walk, on Linux, in seconds. Its self-test takes 21 known cures out of a copy, one at a time, and the stories about them must go red: 18 cases above name it as a guard for that reason, and one more whose cure its stories brought about. Nine open cases name it because their stories are red and listed, and the run demands that a line goes when its story turns green. Neither `make check` nor CI starts it yet, so the page marks it "by hand"; the day one of them does, those cases are guarded without a Mac. It plays below the seam what the stand-ins cannot. *Stand-ins play it* stays about what the controller's tests meet, so such a case goes on saying "cannot".

- **A stand-in made as rude as a Mac** (on its way to the trunk) ends all 49 scenarios and 70 replayed walks in the same state as the polite one. Of the 41 lines of tests that fail under it, 26 pin a courtesy of the stand-in's; five are faults of Arbor's, entered above as found by a rude stand-in only. The rule that cured most of its own excess: what Arbor asked for comes true before the next thing a hand, an app or macOS does; only two commands or two keys follow each other faster.

- **What the night of 2026-10-15 taught about method.** A probe that is invalid has to say so loudly: a round whose own premises did not hold was called invalid and counted for nothing, neither green nor red. And a control on both sides, nobody running and Arbor without taps, told two kinds of hole apart, the poster's and the tapper's, and took back two sentences that had been reported as findings within the hour before: that holes of three seconds and more were Arbor's, and that its main thread had stood still meanwhile. Both had been read out of a log that was merely silent.

- **This ledger's lesson of its first round, met again.** A committed file of what the model's layer heard had its milliseconds move with a change of the controller's timing, 34 lines with the same reports: a file that depends on more than it is about makes other people's runs fail.
## The hosted Macs
What the outputs of runs on 2026-10-14 show, label `macos-26` unless it says otherwise. `docs/TESTING.md` has the short form.
**The machine**
- macOS 26.6.2 on a virtual Apple M1: arm64, 3 cores, 7 GiB of memory, 95 GiB free. bash 3.2.57, Python 3.14.

- One display, 1024×768 points at scale 1. Visible frame (0,31 1024×674): the Dock takes 63 points. The display's identifier is the same on every Mac. The display can be switched to 1600×900 with a helper tool; there is no 1440×900.

- A script's own work begins six to seven minutes after the Mac started, with load averages above 30. Nobody has ever touched the Mac: the time since the last input equals the uptime. The pointer starts at (10,10), and no app has the keyboard.
- On the console, not locked, display awake, no screen saver. Display sleep and sleep are 0: these Macs do not sleep.
- Accessibility and Screen Recording are granted to the runner's child processes. An app bundle signed afresh and started through `open` is not trusted.
- Four event taps of system processes exist before Arbor starts, two of them enabled.
- Black wallpaper, light appearance, Finder in front.

- Every material of an effect view is drawn as one flat colour, (228,228,228) in light and (38,38,38) in dark, over any wallpaper. macOS's own menus and the Dock do tint. Blur and translucency cannot be judged there.
- A plain window's title bar is 28 points high.
**Defaults**

- `com.apple.WindowManager` holds none of `EnableTilingByEdgeDrag`, `EnableTopTilingByEdgeDrag`, `EnableTilingOptionAccelerator`, `EnableTiledWindowMargins`, `EnableStandardClickToShowDesktop`. - `AppleActionOnDoubleClick` is not set: a double-click on a title bar fills the screen.
- Reduce Motion is on, so Arbor shows no motion unless a script switches it off first.
- Displays have separate Spaces. VoiceOver is off. One input source, U.S.
